q: A person has fallen down with sudden loss of consciousness. On examinations his vitals are stable with right eyeball deviated downwards, outwards. Also, pupils are not contracting on projection of light. Where is the position of haemorrhage likely?
e:
Mid brain at superior colliculus
Explanation
Eye deviated down and out with a fixed, non-reacting pupil means the oculomotor nerve (CN III) is damaged. Its nucleus lies in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus.
Key points
• CN III nucleus: midbrain, superior colliculus level; CN IV nucleus: inferior colliculus level.
• CN III palsy: ptosis, eye down and out, dilated pupil, loss of light reflex.
• Pupil constriction (light reflex) is carried by the parasympathetic fibres of CN III (Edinger-Westphal).
• Weber syndrome: midbrain lesion with ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral hemiplegia.

q: A Border security officer had gone for the casual walk. Suddenly a loud bomb blast was there is nearby area and he survived without any injuries. On examination his ears both are functionally normal. Which of the nucleus acts as a centre for the reflex that protected his internal ear?
e:
Superior olivary nucleus
Explanation
The acoustic (stapedius and tensor tympani) reflex protects the inner ear from loud sounds. Its centre is the superior olivary nucleus, which sends impulses to the facial and trigeminal motor nuclei.
Key points
• Loud sound makes stapedius (CN VII) and tensor tympani (CN V3) contract and dampen ossicle movement.
• Superior olivary nucleus is part of the auditory pathway in the pons; it also helps sound localisation.
• Stapedius paralysis (facial nerve palsy) causes hyperacusis.
• Inferior olivary nucleus is in the medulla and connects to the cerebellum, not hearing.

q: A 2-day old new born male baby was brought to the paediatrician by his parents with a complaint of cleft upper lip in right side. Which of the following structures fusion is not there for the given condition?
e:
Maxillary and medial nasal process
Explanation
A cleft upper lip is caused by failure of fusion of the maxillary process with the medial nasal process. Fusion of maxillary and mandibular processes forms the corner of the mouth, so it is not involved in cleft lip.
Key points
• Upper lip: philtrum from medial nasal (intermaxillary segment); sides from the maxillary processes.
• Cleft lip is more common on the left side and in males; cleft palate is more common in females.
• Failure of maxillary and lateral nasal process fusion causes oblique facial cleft.
• Failure of maxillary and mandibular fusion causes macrostomia (wide mouth).

q: A person had come to emergency department with his mouth opened and locked jaw. This had happened during excessive yawning. Which of the following muscles are responsible for the given condition?
e:
Excessive yawning causes an anterior dislocation of the TMJ because the lateral pterygoid pulls the condyle forward out of the glenoid fossa. The jaw stays open and locked.
Key points
• Lateral pterygoid is the only muscle that opens (depresses) the mandible and protrudes it.
• Closing muscles: masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid.
• All muscles of mastication are supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).
• Dislocation is treated by pushing the mandible downwards and backwards (Hippocratic method).
Lateral pterygoid | Medial pterygoid | Masseter / Temporalis
Main action | Opens, protrudes jaw | Closes jaw | Closes jaw
Side to side | Yes (chewing) | Yes | Temporalis retracts
Dislocation | Causes anterior dislocation | No | No

q: The given image defect is due to failure of closure of which embryological structure?
e:
The picture shows a defect between the aorta and pulmonary trunk, a patent ductus arteriosus. The ductus arteriosus is formed from the left VI arch artery, and it fails to close.
Key points
• Ductus arteriosus is the distal part of the left 6th arch artery.
• Left 4th arch forms the arch of aorta; right 4th arch forms the right subclavian proximal part.
• PDA gives a continuous machinery murmur; the ductus normally closes to form ligamentum arteriosum.
• PDA is common in rubella and premature babies; closed with indomethacin, kept open with prostaglandin E1.

q: A 75-year-old male with known diabetic and known hypertensive had a complaint of continuous dribbling of urine and faecal matter without his intervention. Also, his right lower limb got paralysed. Which of the following artery gets blocked?
e:
Paralysis of the opposite lower limb with loss of voluntary control of bladder and bowel (dribbling) is the typical picture of anterior cerebral artery infarct. The ACA supplies the medial surface including the leg area and paracentral lobule.
Key points
• ACA supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes: lower limb motor and sensory area.
• Paracentral lobule controls bladder and bowel, so ACA stroke gives incontinence.
• MCA stroke: face and arm weakness more than leg, aphasia (dominant side).
• PCA stroke: contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

q: A person had right cervical tumour and had undergone for radical neck dissection. Poster operatively a thick white coloured fluid is observed through the drainage tube. The fluid is sent for biochemical examination and diagnosed that they are rich in triglycerides. Which of the following structure might have damaged in this case?
e:
Right lymphatic duct
Explanation
The right lymphatic duct drains the right side of the head and neck, right arm and right thorax. Damage during a right neck dissection leads to a chyle-like milky leak through the drain.
Key points
• Right lymphatic duct is formed at the root of the neck by right jugular, subclavian and bronchomediastinal trunks.
• It drains into the junction of right internal jugular and right subclavian veins.
• Thoracic duct drains the rest of the body, including both lower limbs, and ends at the left venous angle.
• Cisterna chyli is the lower dilated start of the thoracic duct at L1-L2.
Right lymphatic duct | Thoracic duct
Drains | Right head, neck, arm, thorax | Rest of the body
Ends at | Right venous angle | Left venous angle
Injury in | Right neck surgery | Left neck surgery

q: A 60-year-old male patient had come to surgical OPD with swelling in the groin. After making patient in s upine position and reduced the swelling, deep ring occlusion test is done for which swelling is present. Which of the following hernia is the given case?
e:
Direct inguinal hernia
Explanation
In a direct inguinal hernia the sac comes through the posterior wall of the canal (Hesselbach triangle), so occluding the deep ring does not stop the swelling. It is positive for the test in an indirect hernia.
Key points
• Direct hernia: medial to inferior epigastric vessels; indirect: lateral to them.
• Direct hernia is acquired and seen in old age; indirect is congenital and seen in the young.
• Deep ring is the opening in the transversalis fascia, lateral to inferior epigastric artery.
• Hesselbach triangle: inferior epigastric artery, rectus sheath edge, inguinal ligament.
Direct | Indirect
Age | Old | Young
Neck of sac | Medial to inf. Epigastric | Lateral to inf. Epigastric
Deep ring occlusion | Swelling still appears | No swelling
Enters scrotum | Rarely | Often

q: A 50-year-old female alcoholic patient is bed ridden patient for the past 1 month with the complaints of abdominal swelling. Also, he had a weight loss and lethargic. On examination splenomegaly also present. Which of the following areas fluid in abdomen gets collected.
e:
Hepatorenal pouch
Explanation
In a bedridden patient fluid collects in the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity. In the supine position this is the hepatorenal pouch (Morison pouch), the deepest recess.
Key points
• Hepatorenal pouch lies between right lobe of liver and right kidney; it is the lowest part when lying supine.
• In the erect or sitting position fluid collects in the rectovesical pouch (male) or rectouterine pouch (female).
• Rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) is the lowest point in a female standing.
• Ascites in cirrhosis with splenomegaly suggests portal hypertension.

q: The given congenital abnormality covered by which layer?
e:
Amnion
Explanation
The picture shows an omphalocele, in which the abdominal contents herniate into the umbilical cord. It is covered by a sac made of amnion.
Key points
• Omphalocele is a failure of the gut to return to the abdomen from physiological herniation.
• The covering is amnion (with peritoneum); gastroschisis has no covering sac.
• Omphalocele is associated with other defects and chromosomal anomalies (trisomy 13, 18).
• Gastroschisis: defect to the right of the umbilical cord, bowel exposed.

q:
An old aged man gone a routine morning regular walk. He accidentally kept his leg over the man hole which got flipped and got impact at the lower most trunk. After 6 hour he had gone to hospital with complaints of failure to urinate, and swelling of scrotum and penis.
Which of the fowling urethra got ruptured?
e:
Bulbar urethra
Explanation
A straddle injury ruptures the bulbar (spongy) urethra, the commonest site of rupture. Urine leaks into the scrotum, penis and perineum, limited by Colles fascia.
Key points
• Bulbar urethra rupture: straddle injury, butterfly-shaped perineal bruising, urine extravasation in the scrotum.
• Membranous urethra rupture: pelvic fracture; urine goes into the retropubic and deep perineal space.
• Colles fascia attaches behind to the perineal membrane, so urine cannot pass into the anal triangle.
• Retrograde urethrogram is the investigation of choice.
Bulbar urethra | Membranous urethra
Cause | Straddle injury | Pelvic fracture
Urine goes to | Scrotum, penis, lower abdomen | Retropubic space
Prostate on PR | Normal | High-riding

q: Which of the following muscle rupture leads to resulting condition in the given image?
e:
Biceps brachii
Explanation
The picture shows the Popeye sign: a bulge in the arm after rupture of the long head of biceps brachii tendon. The muscle belly retracts distally.
Key points
• Long head of biceps rupture is the commonest tendon rupture of the upper limb.
• Biceps is a flexor of elbow and the strongest supinator of the forearm.
• Nerve supply of biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis: musculocutaneous nerve.
• Triceps is supplied by the radial nerve.

q: A man falls on an outstretched hand with loss of abduction at shoulder joint and upper lateral cutaneous sensations. Which of the following part of humerus got fractured?
e:
Surgical neck of humerus
Explanation
Fall on an outstretched hand with fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus damages the axillary nerve. This causes loss of shoulder abduction (deltoid) and loss of sensation over the lateral shoulder (regimental badge area).
Key points
• Axillary nerve (C5, C6) winds round the surgical neck and supplies deltoid and teres minor.
• Anterior dislocation of shoulder also injures the axillary nerve.
• Shaft of humerus fracture injures the radial nerve (wrist drop).
• Medial epicondyle fracture injures the ulnar nerve.
Site of fracture / injury | Nerve | Deficit
Surgical neck | Humerus | Axillary | No abduction, badge numbness
Shaft | Humerus | Radial | Wrist drop
Medial epicondyle | Humerus | Ulnar | Claw hand
Supracondylar | Humerus | Median (anterior interosseous) | Weak pinch

q: A 45-year-old person on standing on right side foot with left foot off the ground, pelvis sags down to left side. While walking he swayed to right side. Which of the following nerve is damaged?
e:
Superior gluteal nerve
Explanation
Pelvis sagging on the opposite side when standing on one leg (Trendelenburg sign) is due to paralysis of gluteus medius and minimus, supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.
Key points
• Superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fascia lata.
• The pelvis drops on the normal (lifted) side; the patient leans to the affected side while walking (gluteus medius gait).
• Inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus: difficulty climbing stairs and rising from sitting.
• Common cause: wrongly placed intragluteal injection or hip surgery.
Superior gluteal | Inferior gluteal
Muscle | Gluteus medius, minimus | Gluteus maximus
Sign | Trendelenburg positive | Trouble rising, climbing
Function lost | Hip abduction | Hip extension

q: A old man undergone for the coronary artery bypass graft. Also, there is incision in the lower limb. Which of the following nerves is at risk for injury?
e:
The great saphenous vein is taken for bypass grafts, and the saphenous nerve runs along it in the leg and is at risk during harvesting. It supplies skin on the medial side of the leg and foot.
Key points
• Saphenous nerve is the longest branch of the femoral nerve; it supplies skin of the medial leg and foot.
• Great saphenous vein passes in front of the medial malleolus: site for venous cutdown.
• Sural nerve supplies the lateral foot and runs with the short saphenous vein.
• Superficial peroneal supplies dorsum of foot; deep peroneal supplies the first web space.

q: Identify the clinical condition given in the image
e:
The picture shows a fetus with absent cranial vault and exposed brain tissue, which is anencephaly. It results from failure of closure of the anterior (cranial) neuropore.
Key points
• Anencephaly is a neural tube defect from failed closure of the anterior neuropore at about day 25.
• Polyhydramnios and a frog-like face are typical; it is incompatible with life.
• Raised maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein is a marker; folic acid prevents neural tube defects.
• Spina bifida arises from failed closure of the posterior neuropore.

q: Identify the marked structure in the given image
e:
Thalamus
Explanation
The marked structure is the thalamus, the large egg-shaped grey mass lying on either side of the third ventricle, medial to the posterior limb of internal capsule.
Key points
• Thalamus is the main sensory relay station for all senses except smell.
• Thalamus lies medial to the internal capsule; lentiform nucleus (putamen and globus pallidus) lies lateral to it.
• Caudate nucleus lies lateral to the lateral ventricle and has a head, body and tail.
• Thalamic stroke causes loss of sensations on the opposite side and thalamic pain syndrome.

q: A patient with severe anemia has a decrease in blood pH and an increase in 2,3-BPG. What change is expected in the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve?
e:
Right shift with increased P50
Decreased pH and increased 2,3-BPG reduce hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen, causing a rightward shift of the oxygen – hemoglobin dissociation curve. This facilitates oxygen unloading to tissues. A right shift is associated with an increased P50.
Key Points
• Right shift: increased H⁺ , PCO˜, temperature, and 2,3-BPG.
• Right shift means decreased Hb–O˜ affinity and increased P50.
• Left shift means increased Hb–O˜ affinity and decreased P50.

q: A patient speaks fluently, but the speech is meaningless. He is unable to understand spoken or written language. Which area is most likely affected?
e:
Damage to Wernicke area, located in the dominant hemisphere, produces receptive aphasia. Speech remains fluent but lacks meaningful content, and comprehension is impaired.
Key Points
• Broca aphasia: nonfluent speech with relatively preserved comprehension.
• Wernicke aphasia: fluent speech with impaired comprehension.
• Both are usually located in the dominant, typically left, cerebral hemisphere.

q: Botulinum toxin produces flaccid paralysis by preventing acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. Which intracellular proteins are directly targeted by this toxin?
e:
SNARE proteins
Botulinum toxin acts within presynaptic cholinergic terminals and cleaves SNARE proteins, which are necessary for docking and fusion of acetylcholine-containing vesicles with the presynaptic membrane. Acetylcholine release is therefore inhibited.
Key Points
• Botulinum toxin acts presynaptically.
• It cleaves SNARE proteins.
• Acetylcholine release decreases, producing flaccid paralysis

q: Cholera toxin binds to intestinal epithelial cells and causes massive secretion of chloride and water. Which membrane receptor facilitates entry of the toxin into the enterocyte?
e:
GM1 ganglioside
The B subunit of cholera toxin binds to GM1 ganglioside on the apical membrane of intestinal epithelial cells. The toxin subsequently causes persistent activation of Gs°, increasing adenylate cyclase activity and intracellular cAMP. This stimulates CFTR-mediated chloride secretion, with water following into the intestinal lumen.
Key Points
• Cholera toxin receptor: GM1 ganglioside.
• Intracellular pathway: Gs → adenylate cyclase → increased cAMP.
• Increased chloride and water secretion causes profuse watery diarrhea

q: After an animal bite, rabies virus enters peripheral nerves and travels toward the neuronal cell body and central nervous system. Which motor protein primarily mediates this transport?
e:
Rabies virus reaches the CNS through retrograde axonal transport along microtubules. Retrograde movement toward the neuronal cell body is mediated predominantly by dynein.
Key Points
• Dynein: retrograde axonal transport toward the cell body.
• Kinesin: anterograde transport toward the axon terminal.
• Rabies exploits retrograde axonal transport to reach the CNS.

q: A patient with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with diabetic ketoacidosis. Which hormonal pattern is most likely?
e:
DKA develops in a state of severe insulin deficiency accompanied by increased counter-regulatory hormones, particularly glucagon. Catecholamines, cortisol, and growth hormone also increase. This hormonal environment promotes hepatic glucose production and lipolysis, with fatty acids being converted to ketone bodies.
Key Points
• Insulin decreases.
• Glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, and growth hormone increase.
• A low insulin-to-glucagon ratio promotes lipolysis and ketogenesis.

q: A patient has elevated jugular venous pressure. The JVP tracing shows prominent v waves with rapid y descent. Which abnormality is most likely responsible for this waveform?
e:
In tricuspid regurgitation, blood flows backward from the right ventricle into the right atrium during ventricular systole. This markedly increases right atrial pressure during the period when the normal v wave is formed, producing giant/prominent v waves. Rapid emptying of the overfilled right atrium after the tricuspid valve opens produces a rapid y descent.
Key Points
• Tricuspid regurgitation: prominent/giant v waves with rapid y descent.
• Tricuspid stenosis: prominent a wave with slow y descent.
• Cardiac tamponade: prominent x descent with absent/blunted y descent.
• Complete heart block: cannon a waves may occur due to AV dissociation.

q: A patient with head trauma develops markedly increased intracranial pressure. Which combination of cardiovascular changes is most characteristic of the resulting reflex?
e:
Increased intracranial pressure reduces cerebral perfusion. The resulting cerebral ischemia produces intense sympathetic activation and systemic hypertension to maintain cerebral blood flow. The rise in arterial pressure activates baroreceptors, producing reflex bradycardia.
Key Points
• Cushing reflex: hypertension + bradycardia + irregular respiration.
• Triggered by markedly increased intracranial pressure.
• It is a compensatory response attempting to preserve cerebral perfusion.

q: Dietary non-heme iron is predominantly absorbed in the duodenum. Which form of iron is transported into the enterocyte by divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1)?
e:
Dietary ferric iron (Fe³+) is reduced to ferrous iron (Fe²+) at the brush border. DMT1 transports Fe²+ into the enterocyte. Iron is subsequently exported across the basolateral membrane by ferroportin.
Key Points
• Principal site: duodenum.
• DMT1 transports Fe²+ into the enterocyte.
• Ferroportin exports iron from the enterocyte.
• Hepcidin inhibits ferroportin, decreasing intestinal iron absorption.

q: During the action potential of a ventricular cardiac myocyte, which ion movement is primarily responsible for phase 0?
e:
Rapid Na+ influx
Phase 0 of the ventricular myocyte action potential is the rapid depolarization phase caused by opening of fast voltage- gated Na+ channels and rapid Na+ influx.
Key Points
• Phase 0: rapid Na+ influx.
• Phase 1: transient K+ efflux.
• Phase 2: Ca²+ influx through L-type channels balanced by K+ efflux.
• Phase 3: K+ efflux causes repolarization.
• Phase 4: stable resting membrane potential in ventricular myocytes.

q: During a neuronal action potential, what happens to the activation (m) and inactivation (h) gates of voltage- gated Na+ channels during rapid depolarization and at the peak of the action potential?
o: Activation gates close; inactivation gates open
Activation gates open; inactivation gates subsequently close
Both gates remain closed throughout depolarization
Both gates remain continuously open until the resting potential is restored
e:
Activation gates open; inactivation gates subsequently close
When threshold is reached, the activation gates open rapidly, producing Na + influx and rapid depolarization. Shortly afterward, the slower inactivation gates close, terminating Na+ influx near the peak of the action potential.
Key Points
• Rest: activation gate closed; inactivation gate open.
• Depolarization: activation gate rapidly opens.
• Peak/early repolarization: inactivation gate closes.
• Na+ channel inactivation is responsible for the absolute refractory period.

q: Growth hormone promotes linear growth primarily through the action of which mediator?
e:
IGF-1
Growth hormone stimulates the liver and other tissues to produce insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1). IGF-1 mediates many of the growth-promoting effects of GH, particularly proliferation of epiphyseal cartilage and linear bone growth.
Key Points
• GH is secreted by somatotrophs of the anterior pituitary.
• IGF-1 mediates most growth-promoting actions of GH.
• GH directly increases lipolysis and has anti-insulin effects on carbohydrate metabolism.
• Somatostatin inhibits GH secretion.

q: During a cystometrogram, the urinary bladder is gradually filled with fluid. Which pattern is normally observed as bladder volume increases from approximately 50 to 300 mL?
o: Marked continuous increase in intravesical pressure
Relatively little change in intravesical pressure
Progressive fall in intravesical pressure below atmospheric pressure
Immediate maximal detrusor contraction at 50 mL
e:
Relatively little change in intravesical pressure
The normal bladder shows high compliance. As urine enters, the bladder wall accommodates increasing volume with relatively little increase in intravesical pressure over a substantial part of the filling phase. Transient rises in pressure on a cystometrogram represent micturition waves caused by the micturition reflex.
Key Points
• Cystometrogram plots intravesical pressure against bladder volume.
• The bladder demonstrates stress-relaxation/plasticity, allowing filling with little pressure increase.
• Increasing bladder distension eventually triggers micturition reflex contractions.

q: In cystic fibrosis, defective CFTR channels most directly alter which ion transport across epithelial cells?
e:
Cl- transport
CFTR is an epithelial chloride channel regulated by cAMP. Defective CFTR decreases chloride secretion in respiratory and gastrointestinal epithelia, resulting in reduced water movement into the lumen and thick, dehydrated secretions. In sweat ducts, defective CFTR causes impaired chloride reabsorption and secondarily reduced sodium reabsorption, producing high sweat chloride.
Key Points
• CFTR is a cAMP-regulated Cl- channel.
• Airways: decreased Cl- secretion produces dehydrated mucus.
• Sweat ducts: decreased Cl- reabsorption produces elevated sweat chloride.

q:
Spirometry in a patient shows:
FEV1 = 1.5 L
FVC = 3.0 L
Which ventilatory defect is most likely?
e:
Obstructive lung disease
The FEV1/FVC ratio is:
1.5/3.0 = 0.50 or 50%
In obstructive disease, FEV1 falls disproportionately more than FVC, producing a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio
Key Points
• Obstructive disease: FEV1 markedly decreased and FEV1/FVC decreased.
• Restrictive disease: FEV1 and FVC both decrease proportionately, so the ratio is usually normal or increased.
• Examples of obstruction include asthma and COPD.

q: A 17-year-old sprinter has progressive exercise intolerance and muscle fatigue. He has mildly reduced fasting glucose and mildly elevated CK. Muscle biopsy shows low glycogen content with normal glycogen structure. Glycogen synthase is inactive despite normal upstream signaling and adequate glycogenin expression. Which enzyme is deficient?
e:
Glycogen synthase
Explanation
The sprinter has low muscle glycogen with a normal glycogen structure, so glycogen is not being built. Glycogen synthase forms the alpha-1,4 chains and is the deficient enzyme.
Key points
• Glycogen synthase is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogen synthesis; it forms alpha-1,4 links.
• Branching enzyme makes alpha-1,6 branches; its deficiency gives abnormal long-chain glycogen (Andersen disease).
• Glycogen synthase deficiency (GSD 0) gives fasting hypoglycaemia and low glycogen stores.
• Insulin activates glycogen synthase; glucagon and adrenaline inhibit it.

q: A 5-month-old infant is brought with progressive developmental delay, excessive irritability, and stiffness of limbs. The child shows hypertonia, feeding difficulty, and episodes of inconsolable crying. On examination, there is optic atrophy and peripheral neuropathy. MRI shows demyelination of white matter. No hepatosplenomegaly is noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
Krabbe disease
Explanation
A baby with hypertonia, irritability, optic atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, white matter demyelination and no hepatosplenomegaly has Krabbe disease, from galactocerebrosidase deficiency.
Key points
• Krabbe disease: deficiency of galactocerebrosidase (beta-galactosidase); galactocerebroside accumulates.
• Globoid cells in white matter and demyelination are typical.
• Tay-Sachs and Krabbe have no organomegaly; Niemann-Pick and Gaucher have hepatosplenomegaly.
• Tay-Sachs shows a cherry red spot and hyperacusis; Krabbe does not show a cherry red spot.

q: A 1-year-old child is brought with severe developmental delay, failure to thrive, and recurrent respiratory infections. On examination, there are coarse facial features, gingival hyperplasia, restricted joint movements, and skeletal abnormalities. Hepatosplenomegaly is present. Laboratory studies show elevated lysosomal enzymes in plasma but decreased activity inside cells. Fibroblasts demonstrate inclusion bodies. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
Coarse face, gingival hyperplasia, joint restriction, inclusion bodies in fibroblasts with raised lysosomal enzymes in plasma and low levels inside cells is I-cell disease. Phosphotransferase is missing, so mannose-6-phosphate tagging fails.
Key points
• I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II): defect of N-acetylglucosamine phosphotransferase in the Golgi.
• Enzymes lack the mannose-6-phosphate signal, so they are secreted instead of going to lysosomes.
• Clinical picture is like Hurler but with normal urine mucopolysaccharides and gingival hyperplasia.
• Inclusion bodies are seen in cultured fibroblasts.
I-cell disease | Hurler syndrome
Defect | Phosphotransferase | Alpha-L-iduronidase
Plasma lysosomal enzymes | High | Normal
Corneal clouding | Mild | Marked
Gingival hyperplasia | Yes | No

q: A patient with abdominal pain and xanthomas is found to have severe hypertriglyceridemia. During review of the lipid transport pathway, the clinician asks which lipoprotein is produced by the liver and delivers triglycerides into the bloodstream before being remodeled by peripheral tissues. Which of the following lipoproteins transport triglyceride from the liver to plasma?
e:
VLDL
Explanation
The liver makes VLDL, which carries endogenous triglyceride into the blood. Chylomicrons carry dietary triglyceride from the intestine.
Key points
• VLDL: made in liver; carries endogenous triglycerides; becomes IDL and then LDL.
• Chylomicrons: made in intestine; carry dietary triglycerides; give milky plasma.
• LDL carries cholesterol to tissues; HDL carries cholesterol back to the liver.
• Very high triglycerides cause pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas.
Chylomicron | VLDL | LDL
Made in | Intestine | Liver | From VLDL
Carries | Dietary TG | Endogenous TG | Cholesterol
Apoprotein | B-48 | B-100 | B-100

q: Xanthurenic aciduria is seen in deficiency of?
e:
Vitamin B6
Explanation
Xanthurenic acid appears in urine after a tryptophan load when vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) is lacking, because kynureninase needs B6.
Key points
• Tryptophan load test: raised xanthurenic acid in urine indicates B6 deficiency.
• B6 deficiency also causes sideroblastic anaemia, peripheral neuropathy and convulsions in infants.
• Isoniazid causes B6 deficiency; give pyridoxine with it.
• B6 is a coenzyme for transaminases, decarboxylases and ALA synthase.

q: All of the following are true about collagen structure except-
o: Collagen is secreted by fibroblasts as procollagen
Lysyl oxidase is dependent on Vitamin C
Glycine is the most abundant aminoacid of collagen
e:
Lysyl oxidase is dependent on Vitamin C
Explanation
Lysyl oxidase needs copper, not vitamin C. Vitamin C is needed for hydroxylation of proline and lysine by prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase.
Key points
• Vitamin C: cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase; deficiency gives scurvy.
• Lysyl oxidase is a copper-containing enzyme that forms cross-links; its deficiency occurs in Menkes disease.
• Collagen: glycine at every third position (Gly-X-Y); procollagen is secreted by fibroblasts.
• Hydroxylysine is glycosylated in the endoplasmic reticulum.
Needs vitamin C | Needs copper
Enzyme | Prolyl, lysyl hydroxylase | Lysyl oxidase
Step | Hydroxylation | Cross-linking
Deficiency | Scurvy | Menkes disease

q: A 3-month-old child is being evaluated for vomiting and an episode of convulsions, Laboratory results show hyperammonemia and Orotic aciduria. Which of the following enzyme defect is likely to be there?
e:
Ornithine Trans-carbamoylase
Explanation
Hyperammonaemia with orotic aciduria means carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis, which happens in ornithine transcarbamoylase (OTC) deficiency.
Key points
• OTC deficiency is the commonest urea cycle disorder and is X-linked recessive.
• Orotic acid is raised in OTC deficiency; it is normal in CPS-I deficiency.
• Blood citrulline is low in OTC deficiency; high in argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (citrullinaemia).
• Treat with low protein diet, sodium benzoate and arginine.
OTC deficiency | CPS-I deficiency
Ammonia | High | High
Orotic acid | High | Normal
Citrulline | Low | Low

q: A pediatric child photograph shows a child with a swollen face, pitting edema over the legs, a protuberant abdomen, sparse discolored hair, and areas of skin depigmentation.Identify the condition
e:
Kwashiorkor
Explanation
The picture shows a child with oedema, a swollen belly, sparse discoloured hair and skin changes, the picture of kwashiorkor, which is protein deficiency with adequate calories.
Key points
• Kwashiorkor has pitting oedema, fatty liver, flaky paint skin and moon face.
• Marasmus has severe wasting, no oedema, and an old-man face; calorie deficiency.
• Kwashiorkor: weight for age is 60-80% with oedema; marasmus: below 60%.
• Low serum albumin causes the oedema.
Kwashiorkor | Marasmus
Deficiency | Protein | Total calories
Oedema | Present | Absent
Fat and muscle | Fat kept | Both lost
Fatty liver | Yes | No

q: A 17-year-old girl is evaluated for a family history of a hereditary disorder. Her symptoms are mild, but genetic testing shows reduced expression of a specific protein despite an intact coding sequence. The clinician explains that the gene is being "silenced" at the post-transcriptional level by a small non-coding RNA that binds target messenger RNA and prevents protein production. Which RNA is responsible for this process?
e:
mi-RNA
Explanation
Small non-coding RNAs that bind target mRNA and stop protein production act by RNA interference. This is the role of microRNA (miRNA).
Key points
• miRNA binds the 3' UTR of mRNA and blocks translation or causes degradation.
• siRNA is also a gene-silencing RNA and acts by cleaving mRNA.
• tRNA carries amino acids; mRNA carries the code; snRNA is involved in splicing.
• The silencing complex used is called RISC.

q: Which among the following controls is an allosteric inhibitor of TCA cycle:
e:
Isocitrate dehydrogenase
Explanation
Of the options, isocitrate dehydrogenase is the main regulated enzyme of the TCA cycle: it is inhibited by ATP and NADH and activated by ADP.
Key points
• Regulatory TCA enzymes: citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
• Isocitrate dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting step and is inhibited by high ATP and NADH.
• ADP and calcium activate isocitrate dehydrogenase.
• Pyruvate dehydrogenase links glycolysis to the TCA cycle but is not part of the cycle.

q: Conversion of Pyruvate to Acetyl COA is mediated by which of the following enzymes?
e:
Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
Explanation
Pyruvate is converted to acetyl CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex in the mitochondrial matrix. This is an irreversible link step between glycolysis and the TCA cycle.
Key points
• PDH needs five cofactors: TPP (B1), lipoic acid, CoA (B5), FAD (B2), NAD (B3).
• PDH is inhibited by acetyl CoA, NADH and ATP; activated by insulin.
• Arsenic and mercury inhibit PDH by binding lipoic acid.
• Thiamine deficiency causes lactic acidosis because PDH is blocked.

q: In kreb’s cycle there is the conversion of alpha ketoglutarate to succinyl CoA by alpha ketoglutarate dehydrogenase which requires 5 coenzymes, which of the following coenzyme is not required for this process?
e:
NADPH
Explanation
Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase needs TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD and NAD+. NADPH is not required, so it is the answer.
Key points
• Five coenzymes: thiamine pyrophosphate (B1), lipoate, CoA (pantothenic acid), FAD (riboflavin), NAD+ (niacin).
• The same five coenzymes are needed by PDH and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase.
• It gives succinyl CoA and NADH; it is one of the three regulated enzymes of TCA.
• Arsenite inhibits it by binding lipoic acid.

q: Anaerobic glycolysis takes place in absence of oxygen with the net gain of 2 ATPs. This process is usually seen in exercising muscles which is the main cause of muscle fatigue. Which of the following is the commited step for this process?
e:
PFK -1
Explanation
PFK-1 (phosphofructokinase-1) catalyses the committed step of glycolysis, converting fructose-6-phosphate to fructose- 1,6-bisphosphate. It is the main rate-limiting enzyme.
Key points
• PFK-1 is activated by AMP, fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and insulin; inhibited by ATP and citrate.
• Rate-limiting enzymes of glycolysis: hexokinase/glucokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase.
• Anaerobic glycolysis gives 2 ATP; lactate dehydrogenase regenerates NAD+.
• PFK-1 deficiency (Tarui disease) causes muscle cramps on exercise.

q: A 19-year-old man comes to the clinic after a large carbohydrate-rich meal. His blood glucose level is elevated, and his pancreas responds by increasing insulin secretion. The liver takes up the excess glucose and converts it into a storage form to help maintain normal blood sugar later during fasting. In which of the following forms is glucose stored in the liver?
e:
After a meal, the liver stores excess glucose as glycogen, which is released during fasting to maintain blood glucose.
Key points
• Liver glycogen maintains blood glucose; muscle glycogen is used only by muscle.
• Liver has glucose-6-phosphatase; muscle does not, so muscle cannot release glucose.
• Insulin stimulates glycogen synthase; glucagon stimulates glycogen phosphorylase in liver.
• Liver glycogen lasts about 12-18 hours of fasting.

q: Laryngismus stridulus is associated with deficiency of which of the following vitamins?
e:
Vitamin D
Explanation
Laryngismus stridulus (laryngospasm from hypocalcaemia) is seen in vitamin D deficiency (rickets) because low calcium makes nerves hyperexcitable.
Key points
• Vitamin D deficiency: low calcium causes tetany, carpopedal spasm and laryngospasm.
• Rickets: rachitic rosary, bowed legs, widened wrists, delayed closure of fontanelle.
• Lab in rickets: low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high ALP, high PTH.
• Osteomalacia is the adult counterpart.

q: In a diagnostic examination, the respiratory tract lining epithelium of a 45-year-old chronic smoker exhibits a transition as shown in the image given below. What term best describes this observed change?

Metaplasia

0.4 is abnormal). A change in cell number, not cell type. It feels connected because it happens in the same smoker's airway as the image, which is exactly why it is the answer.

Vitamin A controls how surface stem cells decide what to become. When it is deficient, they switch to squamous: the same change as in the image, just triggered by nutrition instead of smoke. Classic sites: eye (xerophthalmia, Bitot spots), airway, urinary tract.
Barrett is the same process running the other way: squamous replaced by intestinal-type columnar with goblet cells, because acid is the persistent stimulus.
Metaplasia is not limited to surface linings. After muscle trauma, connective tissue cells turn into bone-forming cells and bone appears inside muscle

q: A 46-year-old chronic smoker presents with cough and intermittent fever for eight weeks, night sweats, and a 6 kg weight loss. Chest X-ray shows a calcified lower-lobe lesion with ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Serum calcium is elevated, and serum ACE is mildly raised. Lung biopsy is shown. Regarding this patient's elevated serum calcium, which statement is CORRECT?
o: It is caused by PTH-related peptide secreted by the tumour
It results from 1-hydroxylase activity in activated macrophages
It is due to lytic bone destruction by metastatic deposits
Serum PTH will be elevated with suppressed phosphate
e:
It results from 1-hydroxylase activity in activated macrophages
Activated macrophages inside the granuloma make their own 1-hydroxylase. This enzyme converts inactive vitamin D into calcitriol, which pushes up calcium absorption from the gut. The key point: unlike the kidney, this macrophage enzyme is not switched off by high calcium or low PTH, it keeps running, so calcium stays high. This is exactly the same mechanism as sarcoidosis, which is why granulomatous disease of any cause can raise calcium. PTHrP hypercalcaemia belongs to squamous cell carcinoma of the lung ,a genuine competitor here because the patient is a smoker with weight loss. But the biopsy shows a granuloma with caseation, not malignant squamous cells with keratin pearls. Always let the tissue overrule the risk factor.
Bone metastases cause hypercalcaemia by direct destruction, but there is no malignancy in this biopsy and no bone lesions described.
This describes primary hyperparathyroidism. In granulomatous disease
PTH is suppressed, because the high calcium correctly shuts off the parathyroid glands, the calcium is coming from vitamin D, not from PTH.
A low PTH with high calcium is the fastest way to exclude a parathyroid cause.

q: In a 35-year-old woman presenting with body pain and easy fatigability, investigations reveal a hemoglobin level of 7 gm/dL. The peripheral smear is given in the image below. Further tests indicate elevated serum levels of homocysteine and methylmalonic acid. Which statement about this patient's neurological involvement is most likely?
o: It is reversed by folate supplementation along with the anaemia
It results from accumulated methylmalonyl-CoA disrupting myelin synthesis
It affects the anterior horn cells and anterior spinal artery territory
It appears only after the anaemia becomes severe
e:
It results from accumulated methylmalonyl-CoA disrupting myelin synthesis
B12 runs two reactions. One converts homocysteine to methionine (folate also feeds this, which is why folate can fix the blood picture). The other converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, and folate cannot substitute here. When methylmalonyl-CoA piles up, abnormal fatty acids get built into myelin, damaging the posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts: subacute combined degeneration of the cord

q: A 24-year-old farmer presents with abdominal discomfort and intermittent diarrhea. He frequently walks barefoot and has no history of consuming inadequately washed vegetables. Which of the following helminths does not typically enter the human body through the skin?
e:
Trichuris trichiura
Explanation
Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) infects by swallowing eggs in contaminated food or water. Hookworms and Strongyloides enter through the skin of bare feet.
Key points
• Skin-penetrating helminths: Ancylostoma, Necator, Strongyloides, Schistosoma cercariae.
• Hookworm infective stage is filariform larva; walking barefoot on soil is the risk.
• Trichuris, Ascaris, Enterobius are acquired by the faeco-oral route (ingested eggs).
• Hookworm causes iron deficiency anaemia; Trichuris causes rectal prolapse in heavy infection.

q: A 22-year-old woman who wears soft contact lenses develops severe eye pain, photophobia, and blurred vision.She reports occasionally rinsing her contact lenses with tap water and sleeping with them overnight. Which organism is most likely responsible for her keratitis?

Acanthamoeba
Explanation
Contact lens wear with tap water exposure and keratitis points to Acanthamoeba. Naegleria and Balamuthia cause brain infection, not typical contact lens keratitis.
Key points
• Acanthamoeba causes keratitis in contact lens users; diagnose by corneal scraping showing cysts.
• Risk factors: tap water rinsing, swimming with lenses, poor lens hygiene.
• Acanthamoeba also causes chronic granulomatous amoebic encephalitis (GAE) in immunocompromised people.
• Treatment of keratitis: topical chlorhexidine or PHMB.

Source | Tap water, lenses | Warm fresh water | Soil, dust

q: A pregnant woman develops cervical lymphadenopathy and is diagnosed with toxoplasmosis but does not take the prescribed spiramycin. Her newborn subsequently develops neurological abnormalities, and imaging shows intracranial calcifications. Which congenital infection is most likely responsible?
e:
Toxoplasma gondii
Explanation
Toxoplasma gondii acquired in pregnancy and not treated causes congenital toxoplasmosis with intracranial calcification and neurological damage.
Key points
Congenital toxo triad: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications.
Maternal infection is mostly asymptomatic or causes cervical lymphadenopathy.
Spiramycin is given to the mother to reduce transmission to the fetus.
Source: cat faeces (oocysts) or undercooked meat (tissue cysts).

q: A 32-year-old man with advanced HIV infection presents with profuse watery diarrhea for 6 months and significant weight loss.Stool microscopy shows small, round cyst-like structures that are strongly acid-fast positive on modified staining.Which organism is the most likely cause?
e:
Cryptosporidium parvum
Explanation
Small acid-fast oocysts in watery diarrhoea of an HIV patient indicate Cryptosporidium parvum.
Key points
• Cryptosporidium oocysts are modified acid-fast positive and measure 4-6 micrometre.
• Causes prolonged watery diarrhoea in HIV with CD4 below 100.
• Infective form is the oocyst, passed through contaminated water; chlorine resistant.
• Treatment: nitazoxanide, plus ART to restore immunity.

q: A 20-year-old student develops recurrent abdominal bloating and foul-smelling, greasy stools after returning from a camping trip. Which clinical condition is most likely associated with this organism?

Diarrhea with steatorrhea
Explanation
Foul-smelling greasy stools (steatorrhoea) after a camping trip point to giardiasis, acquired from water contaminated with cysts; it causes diarrhoea with malabsorption.
Key points
• Giardia lamblia: pear-shaped trophozoite with 'falling leaf' motility; infective form is the cyst.
• Diagnosis: stool microscopy for cysts or trophozoites, or stool antigen test.
• Treatment: metronidazole or tinidazole.
• Giardia does not invade tissue, so there is no blood in stool.

q: A patient with Plasmodium vivax malaria is treated to prevent future relapses from dormant hepatic forms. The chosen drug also has activity against gametocytes and therefore helps reduce transmission. Which drug has both of these properties?

Primaquine kills dormant hypnozoites in the liver (radical cure) and also kills gametocytes. Chloroquine and artesunate act on blood stages only.

q: A 19-year-old college student develops low-grade fever, headache, malaise, and a persistent dry cough. Chest imaging suggests atypical pneumonia, and sputum culture demonstrates characteristic “fried-egg” colonies. Which antibiotic is most appropriate for treatment?
e:
'Fried-egg' colonies indicate Mycoplasma pneumoniae (atypical pneumonia). It has no cell wall, so beta-lactams fail and a macrolide such as azithromycin is used.
Key points
• Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall; it does not stain with Gram stain.
• Grows on PPLO agar with fried-egg colonies; cold agglutinins are positive.
• Drugs of choice: macrolides, doxycycline, fluoroquinolones.
• Beta-lactams and vancomycin are useless as they act on the cell wall.

Novobiocin | Sensitive | Sensitive | Resistant
Typical site | Skin, pus | Catheters | Young woman UTI

q: A patient develops fever, abdominal cramps, and bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked chicken. Stool culture on selective medium under microaerophilic conditions at 42°C shows a curved, Gram-negative, highly motile bacillus. Which organism is most likely responsible?
e:
Campylobacter jejuni
Explanation
Bloody diarrhoea after chicken with a curved motile bacillus growing at 42 degrees C microaerophilically is Campylobacter jejuni.
Key points
• Campylobacter shows darting motility and gull-wing shape on Gram stain.
• Grows on Skirrow or Campy-BAP medium at 42 degrees C, microaerophilic.
• Main source: undercooked poultry; it is the commonest bacterial cause of gastroenteritis.
• Complication: Guillain-Barre syndrome; treat with azithromycin.

q: A patient with previously diagnosed rheumatic heart disease develops fever and a new murmur following a dental extraction. Blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in chains that are α-hemolytic and optochin resistant. Which organism is most likely responsible?
e:
Viridans streptococci
Explanation
Gram-positive alpha-haemolytic, optochin-resistant cocci causing endocarditis after dental work are viridans streptococci.
Key points
• Viridans streptococci are the commonest cause of subacute bacterial endocarditis on damaged valves.
• Optochin resistant and bile insoluble, unlike Streptococcus pneumoniae.
• They live in the oral cavity; dental procedures cause transient bacteraemia.
• S. mutans causes dental caries; S. sanguis is commonly found in endocarditis.

q: A 25-year-old man presents with pain, redness, photophobia, and decreased vision in his right eye. Examination shows circumciliary congestion, keratic precipitates, anterior chamber cells and flare, and a miotic pupil. Physician decides to add a drug that can prevent the formation of posterior synechiae between the iris and lens?
e:
Long-acting antimuscarinic cycloplegic–mydriatic.
Produces pupillary dilation and cycloplegia.
Used in anterior uveitis to prevent posterior synechiae between the iris margin and lens. Also relieves ciliary muscle spasm, thereby reducing ocular pain.
Golden Points
• Anterior uveitis: pain + redness + photophobia + decreased vision; examination may show circumciliary congestion, keratic precipitates, anterior chamber cells/flare, and a miotic pupil.
• Posterior synechia = adhesion between the iris margin and lens.
• Cycloplegic–mydriatics such as atropine are used to:
• Prevent posterior synechiae
• Relieve painful ciliary muscle spasm.
• Main treatment of ocular inflammation → Topical corticosteroids.
• Anterior uveitis → Steroid for inflammation + Atropine/cycloplegic to prevent posterior synechiae and relieve ciliary spasm.

q: A 36-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of severe pounding headache, palpitations, and marked elevation of blood pressure. During one such episode, his blood pressure is 220/120 mmHg, while between attacks it falls substantially. Further evaluation reveals an adrenal mass, and surgical removal is planned. Which of the following drugs is used preoperatively to decrease the blood pressure in this patient?
e:
Phenoxybenzamine
Irreversible, nonselective α-adrenergic blocker.
Used for preoperative preparation before surgical treatment of pheochromocytoma
Golden Points
• Pheochromocytoma → episodic severe hypertension; surgical treatment is usual.
• Preoperative drug → Phenoxybenzamine, commonly started 1–3 weeks before surgery.
• Phenoxybenzamine = irreversible nonselective α-blocker; Phentolamine = reversible competitive nonselective α-blocker.
• Pheochromocytoma → α-blocker first, β-blocker later if required. Never β-blocker first.
• Phentolamine is used for hypertensive crises due to clonidine withdrawal and the tyramine “cheese reaction” with nonselective MAO inhibitors.
• Methyldopa → hypertension in pregnancy.

q: A 29-year-old previously healthy man travels to a high-altitude region and ascends rapidly without adequate acclimatization. Within a short period, he develops a severe headache, nausea, shortness of breath, and marked difficulty sleeping. His companions notice that he has become increasingly irritable and is making inappropriate decisions with impaired judgment. What is the best immediate treatment for this patient?
e:
Immediate descent
Golden Points
• Acute exposure to high altitude → headache + nausea + dyspnea + sleep disturbance + impaired judgment → think acute mountain sickness.
• Severe disease can progress to pulmonary edema and cerebral edema.
• Severe/worsening mountain sickness → immediate descent ± supplemental O˛ / increased ambient pressure.
• Acetazolamide → useful for prevention and symptomatic relief of altitude sickness.
• Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor; the beneficial effect in altitude sickness may relate to induction of metabolic acidosis, which promotes ventilation.
• Dexamethasone may also be helpful, and prophylaxis includes slow ascent, adequate hydration, and acetazolamide or dexamethasone.

q: A 26-year-old woman with Drug sensitive Pulmonary Tuberculosis is started on a first-line antitubercular regimen under the National TB Elimination Programme. She has been using a combined oral contraceptive pill for contraception and reports excellent compliance without missing any doses. Three months after starting antitubercular therapy, she develops amenorrhea, nausea, and breast tenderness. A urine pregnancy test is positive. She confirms that she has continued her oral contraceptive regularly. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the failure of oral contraception in this patient?
e:
Enzyme induction
Rifampicin potently induces CYP enzymes. This increases the metabolism of many drugs, including components of hormonal contraception, thereby reducing contraceptive effectiveness.
Golden Points
• Rifampicin → potent CYP enzyme inducer → ↑ drug metabolism → ↓ drug concentration/effect.
• Physiological antagonism → two agents produce opposite physiological effects by acting through different receptors/pathways.
• Pharmacological/receptor antagonism → antagonist acts at the same receptor system as the agonist; competitive antagonists compete for the same binding site.

q: A 21-year-old woman develops fever and body ache and has been taking an over-the-counter NSAID drug with marked analgesic and antipyretic actions but only weak anti-inflammatory activity. Following an emotional crisis, she intentionally ingests a large number of tablets in a self-harm attempt and is brought to the emergency department soon afterward. The treating physician identifies the overdose and starts the specific antidote within 8 hours of ingestion. What is the principal mechanism of action of this antidote?
e:
It replenishes glutathione levels
The antidote is N-acetylcysteine (NAC). It replenishes hepatic glutathione (GSH) and can also act as a glutathione substitute, thereby helping detoxify the toxic metabolite NAPQI formed because of paracetamol poisoning.
Golden Points
• Acetaminophen/paracetamol → analgesic + antipyretic with only weak anti-inflammatory activity.
• Overdose → glutathione depletion → excess NAPQI → hepatocellular injury.
• Antidote → N-acetylcysteine (NAC) → replenishes GSH + can directly conjugate NAPQI.
• Rumack–Matthew nomogram → predicts risk of hepatotoxicity
• Aspirin → Samter triad, Reye syndrome ,Hyperuricemia.
• Aspirin/salicylate toxicity → urinary alkalinization with IV sodium bicarbonate to enhance salicylate elimination; severe poisoning may require hemodialysis.

q: A 35-year-old woman presents with progressively worsening exercise intolerance and marked limitation of physical activity. She now develops symptoms even with ordinary activity. After detailed cardiopulmonary evaluation, she is diagnosed with pulmonary arterial hypertension. The physician decides to start an oral endothelin receptor antagonist that competitively blocks both ETA and ETB receptors. Which of the following is the most likely drug?
e:
Bosentan
Bosentan is an orally effective competitive antagonist of both ETA and ETB receptors and is used in PAH.
Golden Points
• Bosentan → competitive dual ETA + ETB receptor antagonist.
• Macitentan → also blocks both ETA + ETB receptors.
• Ambrisentan → relatively selective ETA antagonist.
• Iloprost → inhaled PGI˛ analogue → pulmonary vasodilation.
• Tadalafil/Sildenafil → PDE-5 inhibitors → ↓ cGMP degradation → pulmonary vasodilation.

q: A 58-year-old man comes for a routine follow-up. His blood pressure is 140/100 mmHg, and urinalysis reveals significant proteinuria. The physician starts an antihypertensive drug that blocks the receptor through which angiotensin II mediates its major cardiovascular effects. What is the most likely mechanism by which this drug lowers the blood pressure?
o: Increases peripheral vascular resistance and increases afterload
Decreases peripheral vascular resistance and decreases afterload
Decreases the amount of blood returning to the heart and decreases preload
e:
Decreases peripheral vascular resistance and decreases afterload
Angiotensin receptor blockers inhibit AT1-mediated vascular smooth-muscle contraction, producing vasodilation and a fall in peripheral vascular resistance, thereby lowering arterial pressure and afterload.
Golden Points
• Angiotensin II → AT˝ receptor → vasoconstriction + aldosterone secretion + sympathetic facilitation + cardiovascular/renal hypertrophic effects.
• ARBs → selectively block AT1 receptors → vasodilation → ↓ peripheral vascular resistance → ↓ afterload → ↓ BP
• HTN and microalbuminuria → ACE inhibitors or ARBs are important antihypertensive options.
• ARBs do not inhibit bradykinin breakdown, so cough is much less of a problem than with ACE inhibitors

q: A 64-year-old man presents with progressively worsening exertional dyspnea, marked fatigue, orthopnea, and episodes of breathlessness at night that wake him from sleep. Examination reveals bilateral basal crepitations, elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral pitting pedal edema, and an S3 gallop. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. The patient is started on guideline-directed pharmacological therapy.Which of the following drugs does not decrease mortality in this condition?
e:
Golden Points
• HFrEF = systolic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Typical manifestations result from low cardiac output and congestion: fatigue, weakness, exertional dyspnea, pulmonary edema and peripheral edema.
• Metoprolol succinate CR/XL → mortality benefit in HFrEF.
• Spironolactone → mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist → reduces mortality in symptomatic HFrEF.
• Sacubitril/valsartan = ARNI → superior to enalapril in the PARADIGM trial and decreases mortality.
• Digoxin → improves symptoms/reduces HF hospitalization but classically does not reduce overall mortality in the DIG trial.
• Digoxin mechanism: inhibition of Na+/K+-ATPase → ↑ intracellular Na+ → ↓ Na+/Ca²+exchange → ↑ intracellular Ca²+ → positive inotropic effect.

q: A 52-year-old man with dyslipidemia is started on a cholesterol-lowering medication. Soon after taking the drug, he develops intense warmth, redness, and flushing of the face and upper trunk, similar to the appearance shown in the image below. He has no difficulty breathing or features of an allergic reaction. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for this presentation?
e:
Niacin
Niacin commonly produces flushing and pruritus of the face and upper trunk. The flushing is prostaglandin-mediated, particularly through release of PGD˛ from the skin.
Golden Points
• Aspirin given before niacin can reduce flushing by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.
• Statins → myopathy/myalgia.Clarithromycin can increase statin-related myopathy risk.
• Statins are contraindicated in pregnancy
• Bile acid sequestrants lower LDL-C and are among the safest lipid-lowering drugs because they are not systemically absorbed and are the treatment of choice during pregnancy;
• Ezetimibe → inhibits the NPC1L1 (Niemann-Pick C1-like 1) cholesterol transporter in jejunal enterocytes → ↓ intestinal cholesterol absorption → ↓ LDL-C.
• Fibrates → activate PPAR- → ↑ fatty-acid oxidation and lipoprotein lipase activity → marked reduction in triglycerides. Fibrates can also cause myopathy, particularly when combined with statins; gemfibrozil has an especially important interaction with statins

q: A 58-year-old man with schizophrenia has been receiving long-term pharmacological therapy for several years. His psychotic symptoms are well controlled, but over the last few months his family has noticed repetitive involuntary movements of the mouth and face, including lip smacking, chewing movements, tongue protrusion, perioral movements, and intermittent choreiform movements of the limbs. The movements persist despite the absence of any purposeful activity. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
e:
Haloperidol
Long-term potent D˛ receptor blockade can produce tardive dyskinesia. The risk is related to the potency of D˛ blockade and treatment duration.
Golden Points
• Tardive dyskinesia → months to years of antipsychotic therapy → orofacial dyskinesia, choreiform movements, stereotypies ± dystonia.
• Proposed mechanism → upregulation/supersensitivity of postsynaptic dopamine D2˛ receptors following chronic dopamine blockade.
• Treatment → VMAT2 inhibitors: Valbenazine or Deutetrabenazine.
• Neuroleptic malignant syndrome → fever + extreme rigidity + unstable BP → stop antipsychotic; dantrolene and bromocriptine may be used.
• Acute dystonia → Benztropine (or diphenhydramine);
• Drug-induced parkinsonism → Benztropine

q: A 34-year-old man presents with persistent low mood, loss of interest in previously pleasurable activities, fatigue, poor concentration, and reduced motivation for the past several months. He also has an anxiety disorder and has been smoking about 15 –20 cigarettes daily for several years. He now wishes to stop smoking. The physician wants to choose a medication that can help treat both his depressive illness and his nicotine dependence. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?
e:
Bupropion
Bupropion is an antidepressant that enhances noradrenergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission by inhibiting NET and DAT.
Golden Points
• Bupropion → depression + smoking cessation. It predominantly enhances dopamine and norepinephrine transmission by inhibiting DAT and NET.
• Varenicline → selective partial agonist at 42 nicotinic ACh receptors → ↓ craving + blocks the rewarding effect of nicotine.
• Nicotine-replacement therapy (NRT) includes nicotine patch, gum, lozenge, nasal spray, and inhaler. It reduces symptoms of nicotine withdrawal.
• Nicotine patch → long-acting/background nicotine replacement; nicotine gum → short-acting NRT useful for cravings.
• Nicotine gum: avoid food and beverages for 15 minutes before and during use. Acidic beverages such as coffee, soda, and fruit juice can reduce buccal nicotine absorption.
• “Chew and park” method: chew the gum slowly until a tingling/peppery sensation develops → park it between the cheek and gum for about a minute → when tingling fades, chew again → repeat the chew-and-park cycle for about 30 minutes.

q: A 48-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity comes for follow-up. Despite lifestyle modification, he continues to have difficulty achieving adequate weight reduction. The physician decides to start a newer small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist that is available only as an oral formulation . Which of the following is the drug being described?
e:
Orforglipron
Golden Points
• Orforglipron → oral-only, non-peptide, small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist.
• Semaglutide → GLP-1 receptor agonist available in BOTH oral and injectable formulations.
• Linagliptin → useful in renal impairment because it is cleared mainly by the hepatobiliary system, with very little renal clearance. Unlike several other DPP-4 inhibitors, it generally does not require renal dose reduction.
• Rosiglitazone → can increase the risk of heart failure, mainly because thiazolidinediones cause fluid retention and plasma-volume expansion.
• Acarbose actually cause malabsorption, flatulence, diarrhea, and abdominal bloating.

q: A 29-year-old woman at 10 weeks of pregnancy is known to have hyperthyroidism. She complains of palpitations, heat intolerance, excessive sweating, tremors, and weight loss despite increased appetite. Examination shows tachycardia, a fine tremor, and a diffuse goiter. Laboratory evaluation shows a suppressed TSH with elevated free T4. Which of the following drugs can be used?
e:
Propylthiouracil
PTU is favored over methimazole during the first trimester of pregnancy. It inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis and, at higher doses, also inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 → T3.
Golden Points
• PTU → preferred thionamide during the first trimester of pregnancy. After the first trimester, Goodman & Gilman describes switching to methimazole for the remainder of pregnancy because of concern for PTU-associated liver failure.
• PTU → important adverse effect: severe hepatotoxicity, including rare fulminant hepatic necrosis and liver failure.
• Carbimazole → converted to methimazole after absorption. Methimazole has a longer intrathyroidal duration and is the preferred antithyroid drug outside the first trimester; it can generally be given once daily.
• 5% Lugol solution → iodide → rapidly blocks thyroid hormone release, mildly decreases synthesis, reduces thyroid vascularity, and makes the gland firmer; used preoperatively before thyroidectomy.
• Radioactive iodine-131 → -emitter used for destruction/ablation of thyroid tissue; pregnancy is a major contraindication.

q: A 64-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, easy fatigability, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and bilateral pedal edema. On examination, he has an elevated JVP, bilateral basal crepitations, and an S3 gallop. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. As part of his treatment for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), spironolactone is added to his medications. After several months, he develops bilateral tender enlargement of the breasts and decreased libido. Which of the following mechanisms most likely explains this adverse effect?
o: Activation of nuclear estrogen receptors ER° and ER˜ with altered gene transcription
Inhibition of CYP17 and CYP11A, resulting in decreased steroidogenesis
Competitive antagonism of mineralocorticoid receptors in the distal nephron
e:
Blockade of androgen receptors
Spironolactone has antiandrogenic activity. Goodman & Gilman describes it as a weak inhibitor of the androgen receptor and of testosterone synthesis. Its interaction with androgen and progesterone receptors contributes to gynecomastia, impotence, and menstrual abnormalities.
Golden Points
• Spironolactone → mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist → beneficial in HFrEF. When added to standard therapy, MR antagonists reduce morbidity and mortality, cardiac hospitalization, progression of HF, and sudden cardiac death in HFrEF.
• Spironolactone → antiandrogenic action → gynecomastia + decreased libido/impotence.
• Eplerenone has much lower affinity for androgen and progesterone receptors than spironolactone, so these endocrine adverse effects are much less prominent.
• Estrogen → ER/ER → nuclear receptor activation → altered gene transcription.
• Ketoconazole → inhibits CYP17 + CYP11A → ↓ testicular and adrenal steroidogenesis.

q: A 38-year-old man presents with fever, chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and loss of appetite. Sputum examination confirms pulmonary tuberculosis. Further evaluation reveals that he is HIV-positive with a CD4 count of 35 cells/mm³. He has no features suggestive of tuberculous meningitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate sequence of treatment?
o: Start ATT first, followed by ART within 2 weeks
Start ART first, followed by ATT after 2 weeks
Start ATT and ART simultaneously on the same day
Complete the entire course of ATT before starting ART
e:
In HIV-associated active TB with CD4 <50 cells/mm³ and no TB meningitis, TB treatment is started first and ART is initiated as soon as possible, within 2 weeks.
Golden Points
• TB + HIV → start ATT first → then start ART early.
• IRIS (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome) is an exaggerated inflammatory response that can occur after starting ART, particularly in patients with very low CD4 counts or advanced HIV. Tuberculosis is one of the infections commonly associated with IRIS.
• Lamivudine, emtricitabine, and tenofovir are active against both HIV and hepatitis B virus (HBV).
• Tenofovir → active against both HIV and HBV and is a preferred agent for chronic hepatitis B because of its efficacy, safety, and high barrier to resistance.

q: A 38-year-old male presented with marked polydipsia and polyuria. Following evaluation, he was diagnosed with diabetes insipidus. All of the following conditions are known to cause diabetes insipidus except:
e:
Central diabetes insipidus follows damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary: head injury, histiocytosis and viral encephalitis all do this. Multiple sclerosis is demyelination and is not a cause.
Key points
• Commonest causes of central DI: idiopathic, head injury, neurosurgery, tumours (craniopharyngioma).
• Infiltrative causes: Langerhans cell histiocytosis, sarcoidosis; infections: encephalitis, meningitis.
• Nephrogenic DI causes: lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia.
• Features: polyuria, polydipsia, dilute urine, high-normal or high serum sodium.
• Treatment: desmopressin for central DI.

q:
A 47-year-old woman presents with polyuria and polydipsia for the past week. Despite restricting fluid intake before bedtime, she continues to awaken several times at night to urinate. Her medical history is significant for menopause 2 years ago. She is not taking any medications. Vital signs are within normal limits, and physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory investigations are as follows:
Na+: 148 mEq/L, Cl-: 112 mEq/L, K+: 3.6 mEq/L, Cr: 1.0 mg/dL, Uosm: 200 mOsm/kg, Sosm: 283 mOsm/kg After 5 hours of water deprivation, urine osmolality increases to 405 mOsmol/kg and serum osmolality to 304 mOsmol/kg. One hour after administration of desmopressin, urine osmolality increases to 1000 mOsmol/kg. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s polyuria?
e:
Urine concentrates only slightly with water deprivation but rises markedly (to 1000) after desmopressin, so the kidney responds to ADH and the ADH itself is lacking. This is central DI.
Key points
• Water deprivation test: urine stays dilute in both central and nephrogenic DI.
• Desmopressin response: urine osmolality rises more than 50% in central DI.
• In nephrogenic DI, desmopressin gives little or no rise.
• In primary polydipsia, urine concentrates after water deprivation itself.
Central DI | Nephrogenic DI | Primary polydipsia
Water deprivation | No concentration | No concentration | Concentrates
Desmopressin | Big rise (>50%) | No rise | Little change
Serum Na | High-normal/high | High-normal/high | Low-normal
Treatment | Desmopressin | Thiazide, treat cause | Fluid restriction

q:
A 32-year-old female presents with unexplained severe hypernatremia, associated with polyuria and increased urine volume. Urinalysis shows a Na+ concentration of 15 mmol/L and Uosm of 155 mOsm/L. Laboratory investigations reveal:
PRA: 3.1 ng/mL/hr (N = 1.0), Plasma ADH: 32 pg/mL (N = 3 pg/mL), Plasma aldosterone: 24 ng/dL (N = 6 ng/dL). Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hypernatremia?
o: Dehydration due to decreased water intake
e:
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Explanation
Very high ADH with dilute urine means the kidney is not responding to ADH: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. In central DI ADH would be low.
Key points
• Central DI: ADH low; nephrogenic DI: ADH normal or high.
• Both cause polyuria, dilute urine and hypernatremia.
• Nephrogenic DI is unresponsive to desmopressin.
• Causes: lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, X-linked V2 receptor defect.
• Treatment: thiazides, low-salt diet, treat the cause.
Central DI | Nephrogenic DI
Plasma ADH | Low | High
Cause | Pituitary damage | Kidney resistance
Desmopressin | Urine concentrates | No response

q: A 32-year-old male presents with fatigue, increased appetite, and marked facial swelling. He also reports development of abdominal striae. On examination, he is found to have hypertension. This clinical presentation is most likely associated with which of the following hormonal abnormalities?
e:
Elevated cortisol level
Explanation
Weight gain, moon face, striae and hypertension are classic features of Cushing syndrome, due to raised cortisol. Catecholamine excess gives paroxysmal headache, sweating and palpitations instead.
Key points
• Cushing features: central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, hypertension.
• Also: proximal myopathy, easy bruising, hirsutism, mood changes, glucose intolerance.
• Commonest cause overall: exogenous steroids.
• Commonest endogenous cause: Cushing disease (pituitary ACTH adenoma).
• First screening tests: 24-hour urinary free cortisol, overnight dexamethasone suppression, late-night salivary cortisol.

q: Pseudo-Cushing syndrome (PCS), recently termed non-neoplastic hypercortisolism, comprises conditions associated with clinical and biochemical features resembling Cushing syndrome. Pseudo-Cushing syndrome is seen in which of the following?
e:
Chronic alcoholism raises cortisol and mimics Cushing syndrome clinically and biochemically; this is pseudo-Cushing. Adrenal carcinoma and Nelson syndrome are true causes of hypercortisolism.
Key points
• Pseudo-Cushing causes: chronic alcoholism, depression, obesity, poorly controlled diabetes.
• Cortisol excess disappears once the underlying condition is treated.
• Dexamethasone-CRH test or late-night salivary cortisol helps to separate it from true Cushing.
• Nelson syndrome: pituitary tumour growth after bilateral adrenalectomy, with skin pigmentation.

q: A 45-year-old female presents with increased appetite and insomnia. She has noted significant weight gain, predominantly involving the abdomen and neck. On examination, her BP is elevated, and she has mood disturbances. Which of the following features is not seen in Cushing syndrome?
e:
Cushing syndrome causes hyperglycemia (insulin resistance), not hypoglycemia. Hypertension, hypokalemia and psychosis can all occur.
Key points
Metabolic features: hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, dyslipidemia.
Cortisol raises blood glucose; hypoglycemia occurs in cortisol deficiency (Addison disease). Psychiatric features: depression, irritability, rarely frank psychosis.
Ectopic ACTH causes marked hypokalemia and pigmentation.
Cushing | Addison
Glucose | High | Low
BP | High | Low
Potassium | Low | High
Skin | Striae, bruising | Pigmentation

q: A 24-year-old woman presents with new-onset facial, chest, and back hair growth along with irregular menses for the past 7 months. She is suspected to have hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome). What is the primary cause of mortality in this syndrome?
e:
Cardiovascular disease
Explanation
The commonest cause of death in Cushing syndrome is cardiovascular disease, from hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidemia with a prothrombotic state.
Key points
• Other causes of death: infections (impaired immunity) and thromboembolism.
• Suicide is also increased but is not the main cause.
• Hirsutism and menstrual irregularity occur from raised adrenal androgens.
• Untreated Cushing syndrome has high mortality; treatment is surgical removal of the source.

q: A 37-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe flank pain for 1 day. She also reports intermittent watery diarrhea for the past few weeks. On examination, she has mild abdominal tenderness, particularly in the epigastric region and left upper quadrant, along with CVA tenderness. Investigations reveal hypercalcemia, and USG demonstrates a renal calculus. Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
e:
Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 1
Explanation
Hypercalcemia with renal stone (primary hyperparathyroidism) plus watery diarrhea and epigastric symptoms (pancreatic tumour, e.g. VIPoma or gastrinoma) points to MEN type 1.
Key points
• MEN1 (Wermer): 3 Ps - Parathyroid, Pituitary, Pancreas.
• Parathyroid hyperplasia is the commonest and earliest feature of MEN1.
• MEN1 gene (menin) on chromosome 11.
• MEN2 has medullary thyroid cancer and pheochromocytoma, with RET mutation.
MEN1 | MEN2A | MEN2B
Gene | MEN1 | RET | RET
Thyroid | - | Medullary Ca | Medullary Ca
Adrenal | - | Pheochromocytoma | Pheochromocytoma
Other | Parathyroid, pituitary, pancreas | Parathyroid | Mucosal neuromas

q: A 45-year-old female presents with recurrent abdominal pain and episodes of bone pain. Evaluation reveals elevated serum Ca²+ levels, and imaging demonstrates bone lesions. Genetic testing confirms MEN4 syndrome. Which gene mutation is associated with MEN4 syndrome?
e:
CDKN1B gene
Explanation
MEN4 is caused by a mutation in the CDKN1B gene (encoding p27). It looks like MEN1, with parathyroid and pituitary tumours.
Key points
• MEN1 syndrome gene: MEN1 (menin).
• MEN2 gene: RET proto-oncogene.
• MEN4: CDKN1B mutation, a MEN1-like syndrome.
• Primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest feature in MEN1 and MEN4.
MEN1 | MEN2 | MEN4
Gene | MEN1 | RET | CDKN1B
Main tumours | Parathyroid, pituitary, pancreas | MTC, pheo | Parathyroid, pituitary

q: A 60-year-old male with a history of HTN presents with new-onset severe headache and unexplained weight loss. On examination, his HR is 110 bpm and BP is 175/95 mmHg. Serum investigations reveal elevated catecholamine levels. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
e:
Pheochromocytoma
Explanation
Headache, tachycardia, severe hypertension and weight loss with raised catecholamines indicate pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting adrenal medullary tumour.
Key points
• Classic triad: episodic headache, sweating and palpitations with hypertension.
• Diagnosis: plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary metanephrines and VMA.
• | Rule of 10: 10% bilateral, extra-adrenal, malignant and familial.
• | Treatment: alpha-blocker (phenoxybenzamine) first, then beta-blocker, then surgery.
• | Associated with MEN2, VHL and NF1.

q: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is an inherited syndrome characterized by tumors of the parathyroid glands, pancreas, and/or pituitary gland. Which of the following tumors occurs in 30 –90% of patients with MEN1?
e:
Pancreatic islet cell tumors
Explanation
In MEN1 pancreatic islet cell tumours (gastrinoma, insulinoma) occur in about 30-90% of patients. Parathyroid involvement is the commonest at over 90%.
Key points
• MEN1: parathyroid hyperplasia in about 95%, the earliest feature.
• Pancreatic tumours: gastrinoma (commonest, Zollinger-Ellison), insulinoma.
• Pituitary tumours: prolactinoma is the commonest.
• Adrenal and carcinoid tumours are less common.

q: Which of the following drug classes is most commonly used for the treatment of prolactinomas associated with MEN1?
e:
Dopamine agonists
Explanation
Dopamine agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine) are first-line for prolactinoma, shrinking the tumour and lowering prolactin.
Key points
• Cabergoline is preferred over bromocriptine: better tolerated and more effective.
• Surgery is used for drug resistance or intolerance.
• Somatostatin analogues are used for acromegaly.
• Calcimimetics (cinacalcet) are used in hyperparathyroidism.

q: A 50-year-old smoker and hypertensive male is diagnosed with NSCLC with brain metastases. He is receiving enalapril and HCTZ for HTN. Investigations reveal: Na + 120 mEq/L, UNa+ 110 mEq/L, Cr 0.8 mg/dL, Sosm 285 mOsm/L, Uosm 350 mOsm/L, UK+ 9 mg/dL, blood glucose 112 mg/dL, and BP 150/90 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his hyponatremia?
e:
Diuretic-induced
Explanation
Hyponatremia with high urine sodium, a urine osmolality higher than serum, and a patient on HCTZ (a thiazide) points to diuretic-induced sodium loss with ADH-driven water retention. Thiazides commonly cause hyponatremia.
Key points
• Thiazides are the commonest diuretics to cause hyponatremia; they impair urine dilution.
• High urinary sodium (more than 30) shows renal sodium loss.
• | SIADH also gives high urine Na and Uosm above 100, but needs a diuretic-free euvolemic patient.
• | Stop the diuretic and correct sodium slowly.

• Criteria: low serum osmolality, urine osmolality above 100, high urine sodium, euvolemia.
• Causes: small-cell lung cancer, CNS disease, pneumonia, drugs (carbamazepine, SSRIs, vincristine).
• Treatment: fluid restriction; tolvaptan or demeclocycline if needed.
