q: A patient presents to the ER with altered mental status and is unable to provide a medical history. Family members report >8-lb weight gain over 1 week, predominantly due to fluid retention. They also report that the patient has been unable to urinate or eat for the past week and was recently diagnosed with small-cell lung carcinoma. On examination, HR is 118/min and BP is 182/90 mmHg. Serum Na + is 93 mEq/L. Which drug is the patient most likely to be started on as per the physician's order?
e:
Severe hyponatremia with fluid retention in small-cell lung cancer is SIADH. Declomycin (demeclocycline) blocks ADH action on the collecting duct and is used to treat it.
Key points
• Small-cell lung cancer is the classic cause of SIADH.
• Demeclocycline causes nephrogenic DI, so water is excreted.
• Desmopressin would worsen SIADH.
• Other options: tolvaptan (V2 blocker), fluid restriction, salt tablets.
• Diabinese (chlorpropamide) can itself cause SIADH.

q: A 37-year-old patient has been diagnosed with SIADH for the past few months. The patient is currently receiving 3% hypertonic saline IV along with IV furosemide (Lasix). Which of the following nursing findings requires immediate intervention?
o: Patient reports increased frequency of urination
e:
Crackles throughout the lung fields
Explanation
Hypertonic saline with furosemide can overload the circulation, so crackles throughout the lungs show pulmonary edema and need immediate action. Na of 136 is the goal and frequent urination is expected.
Key points
• Hypertonic saline is used for severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma).
• Furosemide is given to remove extra water and prevent volume overload.
• Correct sodium slowly: not more than 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours.
• Rapid correction causes osmotic demyelination syndrome.

q: A 45-year-old female presents with persistent headaches and episodic palpitations. She reports generalized weakness and increased urination for the past few months. On examination, her BP is 160/100 mmHg. Laboratory investigations reveal hypokalemia. Which of the following is the least likely finding associated with her condition?
e:
Hypertension, headache, weakness, polyuria and hypokalemia suggest primary aldosteronism. Oedema is not seen because of aldosterone escape.
Key points
• Aldosterone retains sodium and loses potassium and hydrogen ions.
• Aldosterone escape stops sodium retention, so there is no oedema.
• Features: hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, polyuria, muscle weakness.
• Screening test: aldosterone to renin ratio.

q: A 27-year-old man presents to the ED with a 2-day history of severe headache and pyrexia (38.2°C). MRI brain shows involvement of the temporal lobe without mass effect. The remaining brain parenchyma is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
Fever, headache and temporal lobe involvement on MRI without mass effect indicate herpes simplex encephalitis, which characteristically affects the temporal and inferior frontal lobes.
Key points
• HSV-1 is the commonest cause of sporadic viral encephalitis.
• CSF: lymphocytosis, raised protein, normal glucose; PCR for HSV is diagnostic.
• MRI/CT: temporal lobe hyperintensity or hemorrhagic changes.
• Treatment: IV acyclovir started early.

q: A 38-year-old female is evaluated for resistant hypertension despite treatment with multiple antihypertensive agents. She reports fatigue and muscle cramps. Her BP is 150/95 mmHg, and laboratory investigations reveal hypokalemia. Which of the following does not accurately characterize this syndrome?
e:
Hyperkalemia
Explanation
Primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome) causes hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia, due to renal potassium loss.
Key points
• Features: hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, low renin.
• Commonest cause: bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, then aldosterone-producing adenoma.
• Hypokalemia causes muscle weakness and cramps.
• Treatment: spironolactone; surgery for adenoma.

q: A 45-year-old female presents to the ED with severe headache, persistent muscle cramps, and generalized weakness for 1 month. On examination, BP is 160/100 mmHg. Laboratory investigations reveal hypokalemia with elevated aldosterone levels. This diagnosis is characterized by:
e:
Low renin, high aldosterone
Explanation
Primary aldosteronism has autonomous aldosterone secretion that suppresses renin, so it is low renin with high aldosterone.
Key points
• Aldosterone/renin ratio is raised in primary aldosteronism.
• Secondary aldosteronism (heart failure, renal artery stenosis) has high renin and high aldosterone.
• Low renin and low aldosterone suggests other mineralocorticoid excess (Liddle syndrome).
• Treat with spironolactone or surgery.

q: A 62-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his wife, who reports rapidly progressive cognitive decline beginning 3 months ago. Physical examination reveals hyperreflexia and an exaggerated startle response. Biopsy would most likely reveal which type of pathological agent?
e:
Prion
Explanation
Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus, hyperreflexia and startle response indicates Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, caused by a prion (abnormal PrP protein).
Key points
• Classic CJD: dementia, myoclonus, ataxia, death within a year.
• EEG: periodic sharp wave complexes; CSF 14-3-3 protein positive.
• Biopsy: spongiform change, with no inflammation.
• Alzheimer disease has beta-amyloid plaques; Parkinson/Lewy body dementia has alpha-synuclein.

She also reports intermittent weakness for several months. Neurologic examination shows 5/5 strength in the left upper and lower extremities and 4/5 strength in the right upper and lower extremities. MRI demonstrates findings consistent with the diagnosis. Which CSF study would be consistent with her diagnosis?
e:
Increased protein, oligoclonal bands
Explanation
Optic neuritis with relapsing weakness suggests multiple sclerosis, where CSF shows raised protein with oligoclonal bands (IgG).

• MS is a demyelinating disease with plaques separated in time and space.
• MRI: periventricular white-matter plaques (Dawson fingers).
• CSF: oligoclonal bands, raised IgG index, mild lymphocytosis.
• 14-3-3 protein is seen in CJD; HSV PCR in herpes encephalitis.

q: A female patient is brought to the ED with altered sensorium. On examination, BP is 88/67 mmHg, pulse is 60/min, and rectal temperature is 34°C. There is an associated history of constipation, dry skin, and menorrhagia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
Myxedema coma
Explanation
Altered sensorium, hypotension, bradycardia and hypothermia with constipation, dry skin and menorrhagia indicate myxedema coma, severe decompensated hypothyroidism.
Key points
• Precipitants: infection, cold exposure, sedatives, stopping thyroxine.
• Features: hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia.
• Treatment: IV levothyroxine with IV hydrocortisone.
• Give steroids first, in case of adrenal insufficiency.

q: A patient presents to the clinic with weight gain, constipation, and dry skin. Laboratory evaluation is positive for anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin (anti-Tg) antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:

Explanation
Hypothyroid features with anti-TPO and anti-Tg antibodies point to Hashimoto thyroiditis, the commonest cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas.
Key points
• Autoimmune; firm, painless goitre in a middle-aged woman.
• Anti-TPO is the most sensitive antibody.
• Treatment: lifelong levothyroxine.
• Associated with other autoimmune diseases.

q: A 28-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance for 2 months. She has a family history of autoimmune disorders. Examination reveals a diffusely enlarged, firm thyroid gland. Laboratory investigations show elevated TSH and low free T4 levels. All of the following can be seen in her condition except:
o: Hurthle cells are found in this condition
e:
Monocytic infiltrates
Explanation
Hashimoto thyroiditis shows lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration with germinal centres, not monocytic infiltrates. It is autoimmune, has Hurthle cells and carries a risk of lymphoma.
Key points
• Histology: lymphocytes, plasma cells, lymphoid follicles, Hurthle (oncocytic) cells.
• Associated with primary thyroid lymphoma (marginal zone/MALT type).
• Autoimmune: anti-TPO and anti-Tg antibodies.
• High TSH with low free T4 confirms hypothyroidism.

q: A 21-year-old man is brought to the ED after assaulting a patron at a restaurant. His speech is slurred, although toxicology screening is negative for ethanol and recreational drugs. His family reports behavioral changes for 4 months, including excessive somnolence, social withdrawal, markedly reduced food intake with weight loss, and declining academic performance. He answers questions with slow, soft, monotonous speech and a downcast gaze. Neurological examination reveals abnormal corneal pigmentation, nearly uniform 3+ reflexes, and abnormal phonation. All of the following laboratory findings can be seen in this condition except:
e:
This is Wilson disease (liver, brain, Kayser-Fleischer rings) in which ceruloplasmin is low, so increased ceruloplasmin is the exception. Liver damage also prolongs the prothrombin time.
Key points
• Defect: ATP7B gene on chromosome 13, with copper accumulation.
• Lab: low serum ceruloplasmin, high 24-hour urinary copper.
• Features: Kayser-Fleischer ring, basal ganglia signs, psychiatric symptoms, hepatitis.
• Treatment: penicillamine, trientine, zinc; liver transplant if severe.

q: A 55-year-old female presents with a firm, painless thyroid mass with progressive dysphagia and hoarseness for several months. Examination reveals an enlarged, hard thyroid gland, and USG shows a hypoechoic lesion. What immunoglobulin is primarily associated with Riedel disease?
e:
Riedel thyroiditis is an IgG4-related disease. It causes dense fibrosis, a hard thyroid and compressive symptoms such as dysphagia and hoarseness.
Key points
• Riedel thyroiditis: stony hard, fixed, painless thyroid.
• Fibrosis extends into neck structures and may mimic cancer.
• Part of IgG4-related disease, with retroperitoneal fibrosis.
• Treatment: steroids, tamoxifen; surgery for compression.

q: A 31-year-old woman presents with a thyroid swelling. Investigations reveal elevated TSH levels. Postoperative HPE demonstrates lymphocytic infiltration with Hurthle cells. Which autoantibody is associated with this pathology?

Explanation

Key points
• Hashimoto: anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies.
• Graves: stimulating anti-TSH receptor antibodies.
• Hurthle cells: large eosinophilic cells.
• Treatment: levothyroxine.

q: A 28-year-old female presents to the ED with anxiety, increased sweating, and tremors. She reports recent eye bulging. Examination reveals HR 110/min and a noticeable goiter. Serum investigations show elevated free T4. Which of the following features is NOT typical of Graves disease?
o: Infiltration of mononuclear cells into retro-orbital connective tissues
Extensive infiltration of mononuclear cells into the thyroid parenchyma
e:
Extensive infiltration of mononuclear cells into the thyroid parenchyma
Explanation
Graves disease shows follicular hyperplasia and scalloped colloid; extensive lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid parenchyma is the hallmark of Hashimoto, so it is not typical of Graves.
Key points
• Graves: tall hyperplastic follicles with scalloped colloid.
• Orbit: lymphocytic infiltration and glycosaminoglycan deposition in retro-orbital tissue.
• Caused by stimulating TSH receptor antibodies.
• Features: goitre, exophthalmos, pretibial myxedema.
• Treatment: antithyroid drugs, radioiodine or surgery.

q: A 42-year-old woman presents with 2 days of sudden-onset anterior neck pain radiating to the jaw. She reports complete recovery from a cold 1 week ago. Which of the following findings is NOT consistent with her diagnosis?
o: Dense fibrosis of the thyroid gland
Plasma cells aggregating around damaged thyroid follicles
e:
Dense fibrosis of the thyroid gland
Explanation

• Subacute thyroiditis: viral, painful, tender thyroid with high ESR.
• Histology: granulomas with multinucleated giant cells, neutrophils, microabscesses.
• Radioiodine uptake is low in the hyperthyroid phase.
• Treatment: NSAIDs, steroids if severe; self-limiting.

After spinal anesthesia, surgeon did palpation of his abdomen again and a lump was felt in right iliac fossa. What is the best line of management in this case?

wait for 6 hours and keep him on antibiotics
Abort the surgery and discharge him
Abort the surgery + CT scan + Conservative management with regular follow up of vitals
e:

Why it is important to palpate the abdomen on operation table after spinal anaesthesia?
• Need to confirm the formation of any lump/mass. Palpation and then CECT
• If there is any mass, then surgery should be aborted.
• Oschsner-Sherren regimen - Conservative treatment
• IV antibiotics + Fluids + Vitals monitoring + Bowel rest (NPO)
• PR/Temp: 4 hourly
• Most patients improve in 24-48 hours
• If abscess is large, 4-6cm – Drain the abscess
• Patients who improve after conservative management: Continue the conservative therapy
• Interval appendectomy is performed >6 weeks
• Indications for surgery: Exploratory Laparotomy
• Rising pulse rate/rising temp.
• Spreading/increasing abdominal pain
• Increasing size of mass
• Vomiting/Ryles tube aspiration increases

q: A 52 year old female presents with RUQ abdominal pain. She has history of jaundice in past. Examination and Lab Investigations reveal chronic calculous cholecystitis. Kidney functions tests and Liver function tests are within normal range. On USG examination, common bile duct is not dilated. Which of the following is the procedure of choice for this patient?
e:
Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy
Clinical Features: Acute Cholecystitis
• Mc symptom; RUQ pain much longer than biliary colic.
• Fever, nause & vomiting
• O/E: Tenderness and Guarding RUQ.
• A mass (GB & adherent omentum) is occasionally palpable.
• Inspiratory arrest with deep palpation in RUQ (9th coastal cartilage) is Murphy’s sign (a/c Naunyn’s sign).
• Hyperesthesia below right scapula (inferior angle) – Boa’s sign
• Mild leukocytosis – 12,000-14,000 cells/mm3
• Mild elevation in S.Bilirubin (>4mg/dL), ALP, amylase & transaminase.
Diagnosis
• USG – IOC
• Findings: Presence of gallstone, pericholecystic fluid collection and gallbladder wall edema (>4mm thickness)
• HIDA scan – gold standard
• A normal HIDA scan excludes acute cholecystitis.
• No filling of GB with radiotracer (99m Tc-HIDA) after 4 hours indicates an obstructed cystic duct.
Management
• Start with IV fluids, analgesics & antibiotics.
• Definitive treatment – Cholecystectomy
Timing of Cholecystectomy:
• Early Cholecystectomy: Patient presents within 72 hours of attack - conservative management and cholecystectomy in same sitting.
• Delayed cholecystectomy: Patient presents after 72 hours – conservative management followed by interval lap cholecystectomy after 4-6 weeks.
• Laproscopic Cholecystectomy – Preferred approach.

q: Three burns patients were brought to hospital. TBSA of patient A is 30% over lower limbs and the trunk, B is 25% around lower and upper limbs and C is 5% around the face. Only one bed is available in hospital. Which patient would you admit?
e:
C
Explanation
Burns of the face are special-area burns, so they need admission whatever the TBSA, because of the risk of airway (inhalational) injury and scarring. Patient C gets the single bed.
Key points
• Special areas: face, hands, feet, perineum/genitalia and major joints; these need admission or burn-centre care.
• Other admission criteria: circumferential, electrical or chemical burns, inhalational injury, children, elderly, comorbidities.
• Facial burn clues: singed nasal hair, hoarseness, carbonaceous sputum; secure the airway early.
• Rule of nines: head 9, each arm 9, each leg 18, front trunk 18, back trunk 18, perineum 1.

q: An adult male is brought to emergency department after an RTA. He suffered severe blood loss. O/E his BP: 90/62 mmHg, PR; 110/min. After basic management of that patient, you are being asked by the senior doctor to send his blood sample for blood grouping, hemoglobin, LFT, KFT, Sugar and CBC. Which of the following tubes would you be using to collect the blood sample?
e:

Explanation
Plain red tube (A) gives serum for LFT and KFT, purple EDTA tube (C) is for CBC, Hb and blood grouping, and grey fluoride tube (D) is for blood sugar. Blue citrate tube (B) is only for coagulation tests.
Key points
• Red/yellow (clot activator): serum for LFT, KFT, electrolytes, serology.
• Purple (EDTA): CBC, Hb, blood group, HbA1c.
• Grey (fluoride/oxalate): glucose, as fluoride stops glycolysis.
• Blue (3.2% citrate): PT, aPTT; black (citrate): ESR; green (heparin): ABG, ammonia.

Purple | EDTA | CBC, Hb, group
Grey | NaF + oxalate | Sugar
Blue | Citrate | PT, aPTT

• Most radiosensitive: Seminoma

q: After a brutal attack on a 16 year old boy, he is brought to surgical emergency with his amputated digit. Ideally, amputated finger should be transported in;
e:
Plastic bag with wet ice
• It is anticipated that the amputated part will be considered for reimplantation, it is critical to transport the patient and the part in an appropriate manner
• The amputated part is placed in a clean, dry, plastic bag, which is sealed and placed on top of ice in a Styrofoam container.
• This keeps the part sufficiently cool at 4°C to 10 °C without freezing.
• The amputated part is wrapped in a lightly moistened saline gauze to prevent tissue drying.
• Ischemic time for digits is upto 8 hours
• Ischemic time for extremities is 4-6 hours
• Organ containing bag should be placed in a solution of saline with ice.

q: A 58 year old male has been operated for carcinoma of caecum and right hemicolectomy has been done. On the 4th postoperative day, the patient develops fever and pain in the legs. The most important clinical entity one should look for is;
e:
DVT
• DVT – Virchow’s triad:
• Stasis
• Hypercoagulability
• Endothelial injury
• Most important predisposing factor: Hospital admission for the treatment of a medical or surgical condition.
• MC site for DVT: Calf or soleal vein
• MC site of DVT leading to pulmonary embolism: Femoropopliteal vein
• MC presentation of DVT: Pain and swelling, specially in the calf of one lower limb

q: A 44 year old man presents with progressive cervical lymph nodes enlargement, since 3 months. Most diagnostic investigation is;
e:
Lymph node biopsy
• In case of lymphadenopathy, if the patient history and physical findings are suggestive of malignancy, then a prompt lymph node biopsy should be done.
• FNAC does not provide enough tissue to reach a diagnosis. So this is not of much use.

q: A 21 year old boy who is an athelete, sustained injury of left ankle. He was immobilized for 3 months. After that cast was removed and patient was able to walk normally. Later he complained of pain and swelling in left calf, left ankle and foot. His mother massaged him for 30 minutes. After a while he developed acute onset of breathlessness and was brought to emergency and died. What is the most likely cause of death ?

• History of immobilization for long duration suggests a probably subclinical DVT that had developed in the patient.
• On massaging, the thrombus of DVT got dislodged in the pulmonary circulation, causing pulmonary t hromboembolism and death of the patient.

q: Fate of paramesonephric duct is determined by which of the following?
e:
Y chromosome
Explanation
The SRY gene on the Y chromosome makes the testis develop; Sertoli cells secrete AMH, which causes regression of the paramesonephric (Mullerian) duct. Without Y/SRY, the duct persists.
Also remember
• Mullerian duct gives uterus, fallopian tubes, cervix and upper 1/3 of vagina; lower 2/3 of vagina comes from the urogenital sinus.
• Testosterone (Leydig cells) keeps the Wolffian duct: epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle, ejaculatory duct.
• Androgen insensitivity (46 XY): testes + AMH present, so no uterus; but no male ducts either, so blind-ending vagina.
• Persistent Mullerian duct syndrome: AMH or AMH-receptor defect in a 46 XY male - uterus and tubes found during hernia surgery.

q: Which feature characterizes vaginal physiological changes during normal gestation?
o: Increased glycogen metabolism in the epithelium
e:
In pregnancy, estrogen and progesterone cause epithelial thickening with increased glycogen. Lactobacilli (Doderlein) convert glycogen to lactic acid, so Lactobacilli increase and vaginal pH stays acidic.
Also remember
• Vaginal wall becomes hypertrophied and very vascular - Chadwick sign (bluish discolouration, from 6-8 weeks).
• Normal pH 3.5-6 protects against pathogens, but high glycogen makes candidiasis more common in pregnancy.
• Navicular cells (boat-shaped, glycogen-rich) on Pap smear are characteristic of pregnancy.
• Copious thick white discharge (leucorrhoea) is physiological; treat only if itchy, foul smelling or coloured.

q: Which of the following represents a virilizing ovarian tumor?
e:
Arrhenoblastoma (Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor) secretes androgens - hirsutism, deep voice, clitoromegaly, amenorrhea, breast atrophy. Theca cell tumor is usually estrogenic; Brenner is usually non-functional; carcinoid causes carcinoid syndrome.
Also remember
• Sex cord-stromal tumor; typically a young woman, unilateral; Reinke crystals can be seen in Leydig cells.
• Other virilizing tumors: hilus cell tumor, lipid cell tumor, Krukenberg tumor (stromal luteinization), luteoma of pregnancy.
• Granulosa cell tumor: estrogenic, Call-Exner bodies, endometrial hyperplasia, precocious puberty; marker inhibin.
• Brenner tumor: transitional epithelium, 'coffee-bean' nuclei. Meigs syndrome (ascites + hydrothorax) goes with fibroma.

q: At what gestational age is congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) typically diagnosed via fetal ultrasound?
e:
CDH is picked up on the mid-trimester scan (about 15 weeks as per key; routinely by the 18-20 week anomaly scan) - stomach bubble or bowel in the thorax with mediastinal shift.
Also remember
• Defect through the foramen of Bochdalek (posterolateral, left side in ~85%). Morgagni (anterior) is rare.
• USG: stomach/bowel in thorax, heart pushed to the right, small abdominal circumference, polyhydramnios.
• Death is from pulmonary hypoplasia + pulmonary hypertension; prognosis judged by lung-to-head ratio (LHR) and liver position.
• After birth: avoid bag-mask ventilation, intubate, pass an NG tube; deliver at a tertiary centre. FETO is a fetal option.

q: Which hemodynamic alteration does NOT occur during normal gestation?
o: Cardiac output is higher in lateral recumbent than supine position
e:
In normal pregnancy systemic vascular resistance FALLS (progesterone-mediated vasodilation). Stroke volume, heart rate and cardiac output all rise; CO is higher in left lateral than supine position.
Also remember
• Cardiac output rises 30-50% - early by stroke volume, later by heart rate (+10-15 bpm).
• BP: diastolic falls most, lowest at about 24 weeks, returns towards normal at term.
• Supine hypotension syndrome - gravid uterus compresses IVC; left lateral position relieves it.
• Heart is pushed up and left; soft systolic ejection murmur and S3 are normal. Cardiac output jumps 60-80% just after delivery (autotransfusion) - danger period in heart disease.

q: Which statement regarding blood volume alterations during gestation is false?
o: Increase is less with low-normal range hematocrit and more with high normal range hematocrit
Increases with gestational age and plateaus at 34 weeks
e:
Plasma volume rises more than RBC mass, so blood volume rises 30-60% and plateaus around 34 weeks. The rise is greater with low-normal Hct and lesser with high-normal Hct - option A is reversed, hence false.
Also remember
• Plasma volume +40-50%, RBC mass +20-30% = physiological (dilutional) anemia; Hb is lowest at 28-34 weeks.
• Anemia in pregnancy: Hb below 11 g/dL (1st and 3rd trimester), below 10.5 g/dL in 2nd trimester.
• Rise is 40-80% in multifetal gestation; it protects against blood loss (about 500 mL vaginal, 1000 mL cesarean).
• Pregnancy is hypercoagulable: fibrinogen and factors VII, VIII, X rise; ESR and WBC count also rise.

q: 22-year-old at 13 weeks gestation reports accidental chest X-ray exposure at 7 weeks gestation. What is the appropriate management?
e:
Fetal dose from a chest X-ray is negligible (below 0.01 mGy), far below the 50 mGy threshold for harm. Reassure and continue the pregnancy.
Also remember
• No increased risk of malformation, growth restriction or miscarriage below 50 mGy (5 rad).
• Typical doses: chest X-ray ~0.0005-0.01 mGy, abdominal X-ray ~1-4 mGy, CT abdomen/pelvis ~10-25 mGy.
• Most sensitive periods: 2-8 weeks (organogenesis - malformations) and 8-15 weeks (CNS - mental retardation).
• Never withhold a needed X-ray in pregnancy; shield the abdomen. Termination is not indicated for diagnostic doses.

q: Which of the following options is considered a presumptive sign of early pregnancy?
e:
Amenorrhea
Explanation
Amenorrhoea (a missed period) is a symptom the woman notices herself, so it is a presumptive sign and usually the earliest clue to pregnancy. Goodell sign (soft cervix), Braxton Hicks contractions and ballottement are found by the examiner, so they are probable signs.
Key points
Presumptive (subjective) signs: amenorrhoea, morning sickness, breast changes, frequent micturition, quickening. Probable signs: Goodell (about 6 weeks), Chadwick, Hegar, Braxton Hicks contractions, ballottement (16-28 weeks), positive hCG.
Positive signs: fetal heart activity on USG or Doppler, fetal parts felt, fetal movements felt by the examiner. Amenorrhoea can also occur with lactation, stress or PCOS, which is why it is only a presumptive sign.
Group | Examples
Presumptive | Amenorrhea, nausea and vomiting, breast changes, quickening
Probable | Goodell, Chadwick, Hegar, Braxton Hicks, ballottement, positive hCG
Positive | Fetal heart sounds, fetal parts palpable, USG visualisation

q: A 30-year-old G4A3 woman has a history of miscarriage at 8 weeks, a second miscarriage at 11 weeks without cardiac activity, and a third pregnancy loss at 24 weeks with preterm delivery due to early-onset preeclampsia. What is the most probable diagnosis?
e:
Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome
Explanation
Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome: recurrent early losses, a fetal death after 10 weeks and preterm delivery before 34 weeks due to early severe preeclampsia/placental insufficiency.
Also remember
• Obstetric APS criteria: 3 or more consecutive losses below 10 wks, one or more fetal deaths at or above 10 wks, or preterm birth below 34 wks for severe PE/placental insufficiency.
• Labs: lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2 glycoprotein I antibodies, positive twice at least 12 weeks apart.
• Treatment: low-dose aspirin + prophylactic LMWH (heparin). Warfarin is avoided (teratogenic).
• Commonest treatable cause of recurrent pregnancy loss; associated with SLE; aPTT prolonged and not corrected on mixing.

q: What is the chromosome number of a partial hydatidiform mole?
e:
69 XXY
Explanation
Partial mole is triploid (69 XXY, XXX or XYY) - one maternal + two paternal sets (dispermy). Complete mole is 46 XX, all paternal (empty egg).
Also remember
• Partial mole: fetal parts/embryo may be seen, focal villous swelling, p57 positive, hCG only mildly raised, low malignant risk (below 5%).
• Complete mole: no fetus, 'snowstorm' on USG, p57 negative, very high hCG, theca-lutein cysts, 15-20% risk of GTN.
• Treatment: suction evacuation; weekly hCG until negative 3 times, then monthly for 6 months.
• Advise reliable contraception (OCPs) during follow-up; avoid IUCD until hCG normalises.

q: A woman with a history of painful genital ulcers 1 year earlier has a 1-week-old neonate with facial and body lesions accompanied by neurological symptoms. What is the most likely infection?
e:
HSV
Explanation
Neonate with skin/mouth lesions and neurological signs in the first weeks, with a mother having a history of genital ulcers, points to neonatal HSV. Treat with IV acyclovir.
Also remember
• ~85% is acquired intrapartum; risk is highest (30-50%) with primary maternal genital HSV near term.
• Three forms: SEM (skin-eye-mouth), CNS disease, and disseminated disease. Diagnosis by HSV PCR (vesicle, CSF).
• Prevention: LSCS if active lesions or prodrome at labour; acyclovir suppression from 36 weeks in women with genital herpes.
• Others: CMV - periventricular calcification, hearing loss; Toxoplasma - hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis; Varicella - limb hypoplasia, skin scarring.

q: A primigravida at 10 weeks of gestation presents with spotting. On examination, the uterus corresponds to 12 weeks. Transvaginal ultrasonography was performed as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
Hydatidiform mole
Explanation
Bleeding in the first trimester + uterus larger than dates + USG with a 'snowstorm / bunch of grapes' pattern of cystic spaces and no fetus = hydatidiform (complete) mole.
Also remember
• Clues: very high beta-hCG, hyperemesis, early-onset preeclampsia (below 20 wks), hyperthyroidism, theca-lutein cysts.
• Treatment: suction evacuation, then send tissue for histopathology; give anti-D if Rh negative.
• Do a chest X-ray before evacuation (lung is the commonest site of metastasis); hysterectomy if family complete and age above 40.
• Blighted ovum = empty gestational sac; missed abortion = embryo without cardiac activity; both have a small-for- dates uterus.

q: Which of the following contraceptive methods is not a risk factor for ectopic pregnancy?
e:
Condom
Explanation
Condoms are protective against ectopic pregnancy (they prevent PID and conception). IUD, progestin-only pills and failed tubal ligation raise the proportion of pregnancies that are ectopic.
Also remember
• Risk factors: previous ectopic (highest), tubal surgery/ligation, PID (chlamydia), IUD in situ, ART, smoking, endometriosis.
• Commonest site: ampulla (~70%); most dangerous: isthmus and interstitial (cornual) - early, heavy rupture.
• Classical triad: amenorrhea, abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding.
• Emergency contraception (levonorgestrel) failure also carries a higher chance of ectopic.

q: A patient at 6 weeks of amenorrhea with a positive pregnancy test presents with lower abdominal pain and moderate per-vaginal bleeding. She is hemodynamically stable. Ultrasound shows no gestational sac in the uterus, normal ovaries, and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. What is the next step in management?
o: Declare as complete abortion and follow-up in 15 days
e:
Follow-up with β-hCG
Explanation
This is a pregnancy of unknown location in a stable patient (no sac in uterus, no free fluid). Next step is serial beta-hCG with repeat USG; laparoscopy is for unstable patients or confirmed ectopic.
Also remember
• Discriminatory zone: at beta-hCG of about 1500-3500 mIU/mL an intrauterine sac should be seen on TVS.
• Repeat hCG at 48 hours: normal IUP rises by roughly 35-50% or more; a slow rise or plateau suggests ectopic or failing pregnancy.
• Methotrexate (50 mg/m2 IM) for a stable ectopic with hCG below 5000, sac below 3.5-4 cm and no cardiac activity.
• Unstable or ruptured ectopic - emergency laparotomy/laparoscopic salpingectomy.

q: Identify the instrument shown below.
e:
Cusco’s speculum
Explanation
This is Cusco's (bivalve) speculum - two blades with a screw and ratchet locking mechanism, used for per-speculum examination with the patient in lithotomy position.
Also remember
• Used for cervical inspection, Pap smear, IUCD insertion and taking vaginal swabs.
• Sims' speculum: single blade, used in left lateral (Sims') position - for fistula (VVF) and prolapse.
• Doyen's retractor: abdominal retractor (bladder blade) used in LSCS and hysterectomy.
• Auvard's speculum: weighted speculum used during vaginal surgeries.

q: Which of the following is not a component of the biophysical profile?
e:
The biophysical profile has five parameters: NST, fetal breathing, fetal movements, fetal tone and amniotic fluid volume. Daily fetal movement count (kick count) is a separate maternal screening method.
Also remember
• Each parameter scores 2 points (maximum 10): breathing (30 sec in 30 min), 3 body movements, 1 flexion-extension, single deepest pocket 2 cm or more.
• 8-10 normal; 6 equivocal - repeat in 24 hrs; 4 or less - consider delivery.
• Modified BPP = NST + amniotic fluid index (AFI).
• With hypoxia, NST reactivity is lost first and fetal tone last; amniotic fluid reflects chronic hypoxia, the rest acute.

q: Which of the following complications is specific to monochorionic twins?
e:
Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
Explanation
Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome arises from placental vascular anastomoses, which occur only in monochorionic placentas.
Also remember
• Chorionicity depends on day of splitting: 0-3 days dichorionic diamniotic, 4-8 days monochorionic diamniotic (commonest mono), 8-13 days monoamniotic, later conjoined.
• USG: lambda (twin-peak) sign = dichorionic; T sign = monochorionic - best seen in the first trimester.
• Other mono-specific problems: TAPS, TRAP (acardiac twin), cord entanglement (monoamniotic), conjoined twins.
• TTTS: donor has oligohydramnios, recipient has polyhydramnios; treatment is fetoscopic laser ablation. Scan monochorionic twins every 2 weeks from 16 wks.

q: A patient at 18 weeks has low risk of trisomy on quadruple-marker screening but high risk of neural tube defects. What is the next best step?
e:
Anomaly scan
Explanation
High NTD risk (raised AFP) with low trisomy risk: do a detailed anomaly (level II) ultrasound next. Amniocentesis is kept for an inconclusive scan.
Also remember
• Raised AFP: NTD, abdominal wall defects (gastroschisis/omphalocele), wrong dates, twins, fetal demise. Low AFP goes with Down syndrome.
• Open spina bifida signs: lemon sign (skull), banana sign (cerebellum), ventriculomegaly.
• Amniotic fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase confirm an open NTD.
• Prevention: folic acid 0.4 mg daily before conception; 4 mg if previous NTD.

q: Which of the following is not included in the quadruple screening test?
e:
Inhibin B
Explanation
The quadruple test is AFP, hCG, unconjugated estriol (uE3) and Inhibin A, done at 15-20 weeks. It is Inhibin A, not B.
Also remember
• Down syndrome: AFP low, uE3 low, hCG high, inhibin A high. Edwards (T18): all markers low.
• First-trimester combined test (11-14 wks): NT + PAPP-A (low in Down) + free beta-hCG (high).
• Detection rate of Down syndrome: quad about 80%, combined test about 85-90%, NIPT about 99%.
• Screening tests only give risk; karyotyping (CVS or amniocentesis) is diagnostic.

q: Which of the following aneuploidies is most likely to be missed during prenatal neonatal screening?
e:
Klinefelter syndrome
Explanation
Klinefelter (47 XXY) has no major structural anomaly and no characteristic biochemical or NT change, so it is the aneuploidy most likely to be missed in screening.
Also remember
• Sex chromosome aneuploidies (47 XXY, XXX, XYY) usually show normal NT and serum markers.
• Turner is often detected because of cystic hygroma / hydrops. Trisomy 21: raised NT, absent nasal bone.
• Trisomy 18: rocker-bottom feet, clenched hands with overlapping fingers, strawberry-shaped head.
• CVS (10-13 wks) and amniocentesis (15-20 wks) are diagnostic; NIPT is only a screening test.

q:
Arrange the following cardinal movements of labor in sequence:
A. Crowning
B. Engagement
C. Restitution
D. External rotation
e:
B, A, C, D
Explanation
Sequence: Engagement → Descent → Flexion → Internal rotation → Extension (crowning) → Restitution → External rotation → Expulsion. So B, A, C, D.
Also remember
• Engagement: biparietal diameter crosses the pelvic inlet. Flexion presents the smallest diameter (suboccipitobregmatic
9.5 cm).
• Internal rotation occurs at the pelvic floor - occiput turns anteriorly behind the symphysis.
• Crowning: biparietal diameter stretches the vulva and the head no longer recedes between contractions.
• Restitution is a 45-degree untwisting of the neck; external rotation follows as shoulders turn to the AP diameter.

q: When is delayed cord clamping performed?
o: All term babies irrespective of birth weight
Vigorous term and preterm babies not requiring resuscitation
All preterm babies irrespective of birth weight
Vigorous term babies not requiring resuscitation
e:
Delayed cord clamping is done in vigorous term and preterm babies who do not need resuscitation; wait 30-60 seconds (WHO: at least 1 minute) before clamping.
Also remember
• Benefits: higher hemoglobin and iron stores (up to 3-6 months), and in preterms less IVH and NEC.
• Small drawback: mild increase in neonatal jaundice needing phototherapy.
• Immediate clamping is for babies needing resuscitation, or with placental abruption or cord avulsion.
• Active management of third stage: oxytocin 10 IU IM within 1 minute, controlled cord traction, uterine massage.

q: A primigravida is in labour. Per-vaginal examination reveals a posterior cervix with 5 cm cervical length, 1 cm dilatation, soft consistency, and the head at −1 station. Calculate the modified Bishop score.
e:
Modified Bishop: position posterior = 0; length 5 cm (above 4) = 0; dilatation 1 cm = 1; station -1 = 2; consistency soft =
2. Total = 5.
Also remember
• Dilatation: closed 0, 1-2 cm = 1, 3-4 cm = 2, 5 cm or more = 3.
• Cervical length: above 4 cm = 0, 2-4 = 1, 1-2 = 2, below 1 cm = 3. Station: -3 = 0, -2 = 1, -1/0 = 2, +1/+2 = 3.
• Consistency: firm 0, medium 1, soft 2. Position: posterior 0, mid 1, anterior 2.
• Score above 8 = favourable cervix; 6 or less = unfavourable - ripen with PGE2 (dinoprostone) or PGE1 (misoprostol) before induction.

q: External rotation occurs after delivery of the head. The head rotates by 45° because of:
e:
After delivery of the head, the shoulders rotate into the AP diameter of the outlet, and the head follows passively, turning about 45 degrees. This is external rotation.
Also remember
• Internal rotation: occiput turns 45 degrees anteriorly under the pubic symphysis.
• Restitution: after the head is born, it turns 45 degrees back to undo the twist of the neck.
• External rotation: a further 45 degrees as shoulders line up in the AP diameter (anterior shoulder under symphysis).
• Deliver the anterior shoulder first (gentle downward traction), then the posterior shoulder (upward traction).

q: While conducting delivery of a 24-year-old G2P1. After delivery of the head, restitution and external rotation occur. During delivery of the anterior shoulder, two tight loops of cord are found around the neck. What is the next best step?
o: Clamp the cord, cut it, and unwind it from around the fetal neck
Try to slip the cords over the fetal head
e:
For tight loops that cannot be slipped over the head or shoulders: clamp at two places and cut between, unwind, then deliver the shoulders promptly. Never pull on a tight cord.
Also remember
• Nuchal cord occurs in ~25% of deliveries; loose loops are slipped over the head or shoulders (or use the somersault manoeuvre).
• Pulling on a tight cord risks cord avulsion, placental abruption and fetal hypovolemia.
• Control the head with the modified Ritgen manoeuvre; check for the turtle sign (shoulder dystocia).
• Do not routinely suction the mouth/nose; dry, stimulate and place the baby skin-to-skin.

q: A 24-year-old primigravida presents in early labor. On abdominal examination, there is subumbilical flattening. The fetus is in longitudinal lie with cephalic presentation, the head is high, and the sinciput and occiput are palpable at the same level. Fetal heart sounds are heard at the flanks. What is the most likely abnormality?
e:
Occipito-posterior
Explanation
High head, sinciput and occiput at the same level (deflexed head), FHS heard at the flanks and subumbilical flattening = occipito-posterior (OP) position.
Also remember
• Abdominal signs of OP: saucer-shaped (flat) lower abdomen, fetal limbs felt easily in front, FHS in the flank.
• Symptoms: backache, early rupture of membranes, prolonged labour, early urge to bear down.
• PV: anterior fontanelle felt anteriorly, posterior fontanelle felt toward the sacrum.
• ~75% rotate 135 degrees to OA (long rotation); ~10% persist as OP. Arrest in OP needs instrumental delivery or LSCS.

q: A 24-year-old woman is in labor with the cervix 3 cm dilated and 70% effaced. A “bag of worms” is palpable. What is the next best step?
o: Put the cord above the vertex
Rupture membranes and confirm cord prolapse
e:
Emergency LSCS
Explanation
A 'bag of worms' feel with a pulsating cord below the presenting part and intact membranes = cord presentation. Do an emergency LSCS; do not rupture membranes.
Also remember
• Cord prolapse = membranes ruptured and cord lies ahead of the presenting part (obstetric emergency).
• Risk factors: malpresentation (breech, transverse), polyhydramnios, preterm, multiparity, high head, ARM.
• Interim measures for prolapse: knee-chest/Trendelenburg, push the presenting part up by hand, fill the bladder with saline, give tocolytics.
• Vaginal delivery is acceptable only if fully dilated and delivery is imminent (e.g., instrumental).

q: What is the most common cause of breech presentation during pregnancy?
e:
Prematurity
Explanation
Prematurity is the commonest cause of breech, as the fetus has not yet turned head-down: about 25% are breech at 28 weeks vs 3-4% at term.
Also remember
• Other causes: multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios, uterine anomalies (septate), placenta previa, fibroids, hydrocephalus.
• Frank breech (hips flexed, knees extended) is the commonest type, ~65%.
• ECV at 36-37 weeks with tocolysis; contraindicated in placenta previa, APH, oligohydramnios.
• Complications: cord prolapse, entrapment of the after-coming head, birth trauma. Manoeuvres: Lovset, Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit.

q: A 28-year-old primigravida is in labor with repeated urge to pass urine and premature bearing down. Examination reveals infraumbilical flattening, with fetal heart sounds heard laterally. What is the most likely presentation/position?
e:
Repeated urge to pass urine, premature bearing down, infraumbilical flattening and FHS heard laterally = occipito- posterior position; the occiput presses on the rectum and bladder.
Also remember
• Compare with OA: the abdomen is rounded and FHS is heard near the midline through the fetal chest.
• Brow presents the mentovertical diameter (14 cm); dorso-anterior positions describe breech/shoulder presentations.
• Management: observe progress, oxytocin augmentation, manual rotation, forceps/ventouse; LSCS for arrest.
• Expect a longer labour and more back pain than in OA.

q: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks presents with painful PV bleeding, reduced fetal movements, increased uterine tone, and absent FHR. BP is 166/98 mmHg, and the cervix is 6 cm dilated and 70% effaced with intact membranes. What is the next best step?
e:
Painful bleeding + hypertension + tense uterus + absent FHR = abruptio placentae with IUFD. With 6 cm dilatation, control BP and do ARM for vaginal delivery.
Also remember
• Abruption is the painful APH (dark blood, woody-hard uterus); commonest risk factor is hypertension/preeclampsia; also trauma, cocaine, smoking, PROM.
• Complications: DIC (hypofibrinogenemia), hemorrhagic shock, acute renal failure, Couvelaire uterus, Sheehan syndrome.
• ARM lowers intrauterine pressure and reduces thromboplastin entry into the circulation, and hastens labour.
• Resuscitate with blood, FFP and cryoprecipitate; LSCS only if fetus is alive with distress or maternal condition demands.

q: A 45-year-old male presents with fever and cough. In a study of 1000 individuals, 150 were found to have the disease at the beginning of the study. After 1 year of follow-up, 50 new cases developed among the remaining population. What is the incidence rate?
e:
Incidence rate counts only new cases over the population at risk. The 150 existing cases are not at risk, so the denominator is 1000 - 150 = 850; 50/850 = 5.88% = 58.8 per 1000.
Key points
• Incidence = new cases in a period / population at risk x 1000.
• Remove already diseased persons from the denominator.
• 50/1000 (option A) wrongly uses the whole population.
• Incidence measures risk of disease; prevalence measures burden.
Incidence | Prevalence
Counts | New cases | All existing cases
Denominator | Population at risk | Total population
Best for | Causation, acute illness | Chronic disease burden
Study | Cohort | Cross-sectional

q: In a case-control study investigating the association between smoking and lung cancer, 200 cases and 200 controls were enrolled. Among cases, 150 were smokers; among controls, 80 were smokers. Calculate the Odds Ratio.
e:
4.5
Explanation
Odds ratio in a case-control study = (a x d) / (b x c). Exposed cases a=150, unexposed cases c=50, exposed controls b=80, unexposed controls d=120; OR = (150 x 120)/(80 x 50) = 4.5.
Key points
• Case-control study gives odds ratio, not relative risk.
• Draw 2x2 table: a, b (exposed cases/controls), c, d (unexposed).
• Unexposed cases = 200 - 150 = 50; unexposed controls = 200 - 80 = 120.
• OR > 1 means positive association with the exposure.
Case-control | Cohort
Starts from | Disease | Exposure
Measure | Odds ratio | Relative risk
Incidence | Cannot be found | Can be found
Good for | Rare diseases | Rare exposures

q: A screening test for diabetes has sensitivity of 90% and specificity of 80%. In a population of 1000 with disease prevalence of 10%, what is the Positive Predictive Value?
e:
33%
Explanation
PPV = TP / (TP + FP). With prevalence 10% in 1000 people: 100 diseased, 900 healthy. Sensitivity 90% gives TP = 90, FN = 10; specificity 80% gives TN = 720, FP = 180.
Key points
• PPV = TP / (TP + FP) = 90 / (90 + 180) = 90 / 270 = 33.3%, so the answer is 33%.
• Diseased = 1000 x 10% = 100; healthy = 900.
• TP = 90, FN = 10 (from sensitivity 90%).
• TN = 720, FP = 180 (from specificity 80%).
• PPV rises with prevalence; NPV falls with prevalence.
Disease + | Disease -
Test + | TP = 90 | FP = 180
Test - | FN = 10 | TN = 720

q: Which of the following does not describe the "Iceberg phenomenon" in epidemiology?
o: Most cases remain undiagnosed in the community
Clinical cases represent only a fraction of total cases
e:
Clinical cases outnumber Subclinical cases
Explanation
In the iceberg phenomenon the visible tip is the clinical cases, and the hidden part (subclinical, carriers, undiagnosed) is much larger. So 'clinical cases outnumber subclinical cases' is wrong.
Key points
• Tip of iceberg = apparent (clinical, diagnosed) cases.
• Below water = subclinical cases, carriers, undiagnosed cases.
• Hidden part is larger than the tip.
• No iceberg in measles, tetanus, rabies (mnemonic MTR).

q: Which type of bias occurs when the study population is not representative of the target population?
e:
Selection bias
Explanation
Error in choosing or enrolling subjects so that the study group does not represent the target population is selection bias. Information bias arises from wrong measurement of exposure or disease.
Key points
• Selection bias: wrong sampling or enrolment (Berkson, non-response, healthy worker).
• Information bias: wrong measurement (recall, observer, interviewer bias).
• Confounding: a third factor linked to both exposure and outcome.
• Randomization reduces selection bias; blinding reduces observer bias.
Selection | Information | Confounding
Problem | Wrong subjects | Wrong data | Third factor
Example | Berkson | Recall | Age, smoking
Control | Randomize | Blinding | Matching

q: In a normal distribution, what percentage of values lie within ±2 standard deviations from the mean?
e:
In a normal distribution, mean +/- 1 SD covers 68%, mean +/- 2 SD covers 95% and mean +/- 3 SD covers 99.7%.
Key points
• Mean +/- 1 SD = 68.3% of values.
• Mean +/- 2 SD = 95.4% (more exactly 1.96 SD = 95%).
• Mean +/- 3 SD = 99.7%.
• Normal curve is bell-shaped; mean = median = mode.

q: A study compares blood pressure of one group taking Telmisartan drug and another group which is on Thiazide diuretics. Blood pressure of both the groups is compared to evaluate significant reduction. Which test of significance is most appropriate?
e:
Blood pressure is quantitative data and the two drug groups are different, independent groups, so the unpaired t-test is used. Paired t-test needs the same subjects measured twice.
Key points
• Quantitative data: t-test (2 groups), ANOVA (3 or more groups).
• Qualitative data: chi-square test.
• Same group before and after treatment: paired t-test.
• Mann-Whitney U is the non-parametric alternative to unpaired t-test.
Data | Groups | Test
Quantitative | 2 independent groups | Unpaired t-test
Quantitative | Same group twice | Paired t-test
Quantitative | 3 or more groups | ANOVA
Qualitative | 2 or more groups | Chi-square

q: The platform that is recently launched which has real time dashboard of all pregnant women and children is
e:
JANANI is the recently launched platform giving a real-time dashboard of all pregnant women and children. SSBSK, PMSMA and PMMVY are different schemes.
Key points
• JANANI is the real-time dashboard for pregnant women and children.
• PMSMA: free ANC check-up on the 9th of every month.
• PMMVY: cash benefit for pregnant and lactating women.
• Remember the platform name for current-affairs style questions.

q: The 4 T’s in anemia mukt bharat stands for
e:
The 4 T's of Anemia Mukt Bharat are Test - Treat - Talk - Trace: test for anemia, treat with IFA, counsel and trace the cases.
Key points
• Anemia Mukt Bharat uses a 6 x 6 x 6 strategy.
• It has 6 beneficiary groups, 6 interventions and 6 institutional mechanisms.
• Interventions: prophylactic IFA, deworming, behaviour change communication, testing and treatment, IFA-fortified foods, treating non-nutritional causes of anaemia.
• Weekly IFA: children 5-9 yr pink tablet, adolescents blue, women of reproductive age red.

q: Which among the following is incorrect statement about programme associated with following logo?
o: Focusses on promoting the concept of Saathiya – an adolescent peer educator
Provision of nutrition to adolescents is the one of the prime strategies
ARSH clinics support treatment for sexually transmitted infections
Mental health and substance misuse promotion is key element of the programme
e:
The logo is of RKSK (Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram). Its focus is peer education (Saathiya), adolescent friendly clinics (ARSH) and mental health and substance misuse; nutrition provision is not the prime strategy of the programme.
Key points
• RKSK covers adolescents 10-19 years.
• Peer educator is called Saathiya; AFHC (ARSH) clinics are the service point.
• Key themes: SRH, mental health, substance misuse, injuries, NCDs.
• Iron and folic acid for adolescents comes through weekly IFA (WIFS).

q: An intern working in tribal PHC has conducted an immunization session and at end of vaccination session has to dispose cotton, vaccine vial and syringe in which bags respectively?
e:
Soiled cotton goes in the yellow bag, empty vaccine vials in the blue box (glass) and syringes without needle in the red bag (plastic).
Key points
• Yellow: soiled waste, cotton, dressings, expired medicines; incineration.
• Red: plastic and rubber items such as syringe without needle, tubing.
• Blue: glass vials, ampoules, metallic implants.
• White: sharps, needles, blades in puncture-proof container.
Waste | Disposal
Yellow | Cotton, human waste | Incineration
Red | Plastic, syringes | Recycle
Blue | Glass vials | Recycle
White | Needles, blades | Recycle

q: National Disaster management authority is responsible for management of all except
e:
Road traffic accident
Explanation
NDMA handles natural and major disasters like earthquakes, floods and chemical disasters. A routine road traffic accident is not managed by NDMA.
Key points
• NDMA is headed by the Prime Minister.
• NDRF works under NDMA and the Ministry of Home Affairs.
• Disaster cycle: mitigation, preparedness, response, recovery.
• Road accidents are handled by local emergency and trauma services.

q: A series of lectures by experts on a topic is known as
e:
Symposium
Explanation
A series of lectures by experts on one theme in front of an audience is a symposium. A panel discussion is a discussion among experts with a moderator.
Key points
• Symposium: series of short lectures by experts.
• Panel discussion: experts discuss with a moderator before audience.
• Group discussion: small group, all members take part.
• Demonstration: showing how a procedure is done.
Symposium | Panel | Group disc.
Format | Lectures | Discussion | Discussion
Speakers | Experts | Experts | All members
Moderator | Chairman | Yes | Leader

q: A pregnant women presented to Subcenter for regular antenatal visit. Which among the following information of RDA is incorrectly given by ANM?
o: Intake of vit - A should be 900 mcg daily
Folic acid intake should be 500 mcg daily
Iodine intake should be 250 mcg daily
Calcium intake should be 1000 mg daily
e:
Folic acid intake should be 500 mcg daily
Explanation
The RDA of folic acid in pregnancy is 570 mcg/day, so '500 mcg' is the incorrect statement. (500 mcg is the folic acid content of the IFA tablet, not the RDA.)
Key points
• Pregnancy RDA: vitamin A 900 mcg, iodine 250 mcg, calcium 1000 mg, folic acid 570 mcg.
• IFA tablet for pregnant women: 60 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid.
• IFA is given daily from the 4th month of pregnancy, and continued for 6 months of lactation.
• Iodine need rises in pregnancy to prevent cretinism in the baby.

q: A farmer presents to PHC with complaints of pedal edema and breathlessness. On history taking the patient gives history of consumption of mustard oil. What could be the food toxicant involved?
e:
Epidemic dropsy (pedal edema, breathlessness) follows consumption of mustard oil adulterated with Argemone oil; the toxin is sanguinarine.
Key points
• Epidemic dropsy: argemone oil in mustard oil, toxin sanguinarine.
• Features: pedal edema, glaucoma, heart failure, ascites, diarrhoea.
• Nitric acid test (orange-red colour) detects argemone oil.
• Neurolathyrism: Lathyrus sativus, BOAA toxin; aflatoxin: groundnut.
Disease | Toxin
Argemone oil | Epidemic dropsy | Sanguinarine
Lathyrus | Neurolathyrism | BOAA
Groundnut | Aflatoxicosis | Aflatoxin
Crotalaria | Endemic ascites | Pyrrolizidine

q: The following instrument is used to measure
e:
The Kata thermometer measures low air velocity and cooling power. Hemoglobin, humidity and chlorine demand are measured by other instruments.
Key points
• Kata thermometer: low air velocity and cooling power.
• Anemometer: higher air velocity.
• Globe thermometer: radiant heat.
• Hygrometer / sling psychrometer: humidity.

q: A 50-year-old truck driver presents to PHC with complaints of genital ulcer on the shaft of penis. The correct step of management is
o: Screen for HIV/AIDS and treat him with Blue color STI kit
Screen for HIV/AIDS and treat him with White color STI kit
Screening for HIV is not mandatory and give white color STI kit only
Screening for HIV is not mandatory and give blue color STI kit only
e:
Screen for HIV/AIDS and treat him with White color STI kit
Explanation
Genital ulcer is managed syndromically with the white STI kit (kit 3), and HIV screening is advised for every STI patient.
Key points
• Kit 3, white: genital ulcer (non-herpetic).
• Kit 4, blue: genital ulcer in penicillin allergy.
• Kit 5, red: herpetic genital ulcer.
• Kit 1 grey: cervicitis; kit 2 green: vaginal discharge; kit 6 yellow: PID.
Kit | Colour | Use
3 | White | Genital ulcer
4 | Blue | Ulcer in penicillin allergy
5 | Red | Herpetic ulcer
1 | Grey | Cervicitis

q: The quarantine period for yellow fever contacts is
e:
6 days
Explanation
Quarantine is restricted movement of healthy contacts for up to the incubation period; for yellow fever the quarantine period is 6 days.
Key points
• Quarantine: apparently healthy contacts, maximum one incubation period.
• Isolation: clinical cases, for the communicable period.
• Yellow fever quarantine = 6 days (IHR).
• Yellow fever vaccine (17D) gives protection from 10 days, lasting lifelong.

q: Most common cause of blindness in 25-year-old patient is
e:
Corneal opacities
Explanation
In a young adult (below 50 years) the commonest cause of blindness is non-trachomatous corneal opacity. Refractive error is the commonest cause of visual impairment.
Key points
• Below 50 years: refractive errors cause most visual impairment.
• Blindness is visual acuity below 3/60 in the better eye.
• Above 50 years: cataract is the commonest cause of blindness.
• NPCBVI target: blindness prevalence below 0.25%.
Visual impairment | Blindness
Below 50 yr | Refractive error | Corneal opacity
Above 50 yr | Cataract | Cataract

q: A public health programme was planned which costs around 10 crore rupees and saves around 10000 lives of people. What is the management technique used in this analysis?
e:
Cost effective analysis
Explanation
The programme cost is in rupees and the benefit is in natural units (lives saved), so it is cost effective analysis. Cost benefit analysis expresses both in money.
Key points
• Cost effectiveness: cost in money, outcome in natural units (lives saved).
• Cost benefit: both cost and benefit in money.
• Cost effective analysis compares different ways to reach the same goal.
• Work sampling studies how staff time is used.
Cost | Outcome
Cost effectiveness | Money | Lives, cases
Cost benefit | Money | Money

q: Which set of combination of vaccines is correct for open vial policy
e:
fIPV and OPV
Explanation
Vials with the VVM on the body can be reused for up to 28 days under the open vial policy, so fIPV and OPV is the correct pair. BCG and MR are reconstituted vaccines and must be discarded within 4-6 hours.
Key points
• Open vial policy: reuse up to 28 days if not expired, stored properly and VVM is visible and below discard point.
• Reusable (VVM on body): OPV, IPV/fIPV, Penta, DPT, TT/Td, Hepatitis B, rotavirus, JE killed (JENVAC).
• Not reusable (VVM on lid or neck): BCG and MR; use within 4-6 hours of reconstitution.
• Discard any vial if the VVM reaches the discard point or the vial is contaminated.
Reusable up to 28 days | Discard in 4-6 hours
Vaccines | OPV, fIPV, Penta, Hep B, JE killed | BCG, MR
VVM position | On body of vial | On lid or neck

q: Aluminium hydroxide as adjuvant is not found in
e:
OPV
Explanation
Killed or adsorbed vaccines such as DPT, Penta and the HPV vaccine contain aluminium hydroxide adjuvant. OPV is a live oral vaccine and has no adjuvant.
Key points
• Alum adjuvant is present in DPT, Penta, DT, Td, Hep B, HPV.
• Alum-containing vaccines are freeze-sensitive; do the shake test.
• Give them by deep intramuscular route, not subcutaneous.
• OPV is live, oral and heat sensitive, with no adjuvant.

q: Medical officer facilities in India are deficient at
e:
Subcenter and Village level
Explanation
Medical officers are posted from the PHC upwards. The subcenter (ANM and MPW) and village (ASHA, anganwadi) levels have no medical officer.
Key points
• Subcenter: ANM and male health worker, no doctor.
• PHC: first contact with a medical officer.
• CHC: four specialists.
• Village level: ASHA, anganwadi worker.

q: Correct statement about ASHA worker
o: Responsible for Village health & nutrition day
Responsible for fever treatment at village level
e:
Responsible for Village health & nutrition day
Explanation
ASHA mobilises the community for the Village Health and Nutrition Day. IUD insertion and delivery are done by trained health staff, not by ASHA.
Key points
• ASHA is a female, 25-45 yr, minimum 10th pass, village resident.
• She is a depot holder of ORS, IFA, and contraceptives.
• She is a member of the village health sanitation and nutrition committee.
• ASHA gets performance-based incentives, not a salary.

q: A medical officer working at PHC should be trained to notify which diseases to District medical health authority as per international health regulations
e:
Small pox and yellow fever
Explanation
As per the International Health Regulations, smallpox and yellow fever are diseases to be notified by the medical officer to the district health authority.
Key points
• IHR notifiable diseases include smallpox, polio, SARS, new influenza subtype.
• Yellow fever is notified to the district health authority and WHO.
• Notification flows from PHC medical officer to district authority.
• Yellow fever is spread by Aedes aegypti; the vaccine is 17D.

q: A 40 year old male presents to OPD with complaints of breathlessness, hemoptysis and chest pain. His x–ray reveals ground glass opacities. What could be the most probable diagnosis?
e:
The history of breathlessness, hemoptysis and chest pain fits mesothelioma, an asbestos-related disease. Bagassosis and byssinosis are non-malignant dust diseases.
Key points
• Asbestos causes asbestosis, lung cancer and mesothelioma.
• Bagassosis: sugarcane dust; byssinosis: cotton dust.
• Silicosis: silica; anthracosis: coal dust.
• Asbestos bodies in sputum are the marker of exposure.

q: During census drive, which of the following would be right combination for joint family?
o: Married couple, children and their parents
Many married couples and their children in which all of the family members are related by blood
Many married couples and their children in which male members are related by blood
e:
For census purposes the joint family is many married couples and their children in which the male members are related by blood.
Key points
• Nuclear family: couple with unmarried children.
• Three-generation family: couple, children and grandparents.
• Joint family: several married couples with male members related by blood.
• Census uses household as the unit of enumeration.

q: If the crude birth rate of India is 18, how many pregnant women can be estimated for a rural PHC?
e:
594
Explanation
Rural PHC population is 30,000. Births = 18 x 30 = 540. Expected pregnancies = births + 10% for abortions and stillbirths = 540 x 1.1 = 594.
Key points
• Rural PHC covers 30,000 population.
• Expected births = CBR x population / 1000 = 540.
• Expected pregnancies = births x 1.1 (add 10%).
• Expected pregnancies = 594.

q: Which among the following is not a component of National Family welfare programme?
e:
ANMOL is the ANM online tracking app, not a family welfare programme component. NISCHAY (pregnancy test kit), Mala-N (OCP) and Antara (DMPA) are family planning items.
Key points
• NISCHAY: free pregnancy testing kit.
• Mala-N: oral contraceptive pill supplied free.
• Antara: injectable DMPA, given every 3 months.
• ANMOL is an ANM tablet-based tracking app.

q: The target MMR for India is
e:
<70/1 lac live births by 2030
Explanation
India's target is MMR of below 70 per 1 lakh live births by 2030 (SDG target). MMR is always expressed per lakh live births, not per 1000.
Key points
MMR = maternal deaths / live births x 100,000.
SDG 3.1 target: MMR below 70 by 2030.
Latest MMR in India is 88 per lakh live births.
Major causes: hemorrhage, anemia, hypertension, sepsis.

q: An 18 year old boy was hit on the nose while playing football and developed deviation of nose. O/E, the septum was not deviated. Which of the following is true about the patient?
o: He should be taken for closed reduction as soon as overlying edema subsides
He should be taken up for open reduction one week later
Septoplasty should be done in the same sitting
e:
• Since the septum is not deviated he is most likely having class 1 Chevallet fracture. Hence he should be managed by closed reduction as soon as overlying edema subsides which generally takes around 5 – 7 days.
• Since the septum is not deviated, so septoplasty will not be required.
• If the patient presents after 3 weeks then the management is open reduction

q: A 2 year old fully immunized child developed sore throat, dysphagia, fever and stridor in quick succession. Within 2 hours of onset of symptoms the child was very sick, pale and looked terrified. An hour later, the child became quiet and floppy. And within next one hour the child expired. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
• Child is immunized – so practically no chance of diptheria
• Since there is fever, foreign body is ruled out.
• Laryngotracheobronchitis can also be present in the same fashion but it being mainly a subglottic involvement, dysphagia is not seen here.
• DYSPHAGIA points towards acute epiglottitis

q: After laparoscopic appendicectomy, patient had fall from bed on her nose after which she had swelling in nose and difficulty in breathing. What is the next step in management?
o: Discharge after 2 days and follow up of the patient after 8 weeks
e: She had possibly developed septal hematoma which has to be drained as early as possible.

q:
A 5 year old child is scheduled for tonsillectomy. On the day of surgery he had running nose, temperature
37.5 °C and dry cough. Which of the following should be the most appropriate decision for surgery?
o: Get X-ray chest done and if normal, proceed for surgery
Can proceed for surgery on the same day after starting I/V antibiotics and paracetamol
Surgery should be done next day and child should be put on I/V antibiotics and paracetamol
Cancel surgery for 3 weeks and put the patient on antibiotics
e:
Cancel surgery for 3 weeks and put the patient on antibiotics
• Tonsillectomy is an elective surgery done under GA.
• Intubation during URTI carries a high risk of laryngospasm and lung complications.
• Also a chance of hemorrhage is increased during URTI.
• Postponement of surgery for 3 weeks and antibiotics are to be started.

q: Post head injury, the patient had conductive deafness and on examination, tympanic membrane was normal and mobile with increased compliance on impedance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
• Intact TM with increased compliance on impedance suggests distortion of ossicular chain.
• Hemotympanum is a possibility following head injury leading to conductive deafness but here TM compliance will be reduced.
• Tympanosclerosis and otosclerosis do not follow head injury and tympanometry shows reduced compliance.

q: A 30 year old woman with family history of hearing loss from mother ’s side developed hearing problem during pregnancy. Hearing loss is bilateral, slowly progressive. Pure tone audiometry shows an apparent bone conduction hearing loss at 2000 Hz. What is the most likely diagnosis?

q: A neonate can respire without difficulty during suckling milk. This is due to;
e:
• In newborns, the larynx is initially at the level of C2-C3 vertebrae, and is therefore higher relative to its position in the adult body (C3, 4,5 AND 6).
• During swallowing, the already higher situated, infant’s larynx reaches C1-C2 and the epiglottis meets the soft palate.
• This makes a separate nasopharyngeal channel for nasal breathing while at the same time, the milk passes from the sides of the epiglottis into the hypopharynx thus allowing simultaneous nasal breathing and swallowing during suckling.
• The larynx descends as the child grows to lie opposite C3 and C4, when nasal respiration and swallowing is not possible simultaneously.

q: A child has congenital cataract involving the visual axis which was detected by the parents right at birth. When should the child be operated?

At 4 years when ocular and orbital growth is complete

Immediately

q: A 57 year old female comes to the casualty with history of severe eye pain, redness and diminution of vision. O/E, the visual acuity is 6/60, there is circumcorneal congestion, corneal oedema and a shallow anterior chamber. Which the following is the next line of management?
e:
Intravenous mannitol
• The first drug to be administered in a case of acute ACG is I/V mannitol or oral acetazolamide. This helps to reduce the IOP by dehydrating and reducing the vitreous volume.
• Following this, pilocarpine eye drops are used to constrict the pupil and break the acute attack. Thus pilocarpine is the definitive drug for acute ACG.
• Finally when the corneal oedema has resolved, the patient has to undergo laser iridotomy to prevent such attacks in future. Laser has to be done in the fellow eye also as the disease is bilateral. Hence, laser iridotomy if the definitive management.

q: A 55 year old man presents after 3 days of cataract surgery with history of pain and decrease in vision after an initial improvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
Endophthalmitis
• ENDOPHTHALMITIS: It is severe & vision threatening complication of cataract surgery. It is a suppurative inflammation starting from the vitreous which extends to all the parts of eye except sclera.
• It can occur in 7 days of surgery. MC causative organism is Staph epidermidis.
Steps to prevent endophthalmitis are;
• Preoperative antibiotic eye drops 3 days prior to surgery
• Sterile operative preparation
• Irrigation of conjunctival cul-de-sac with povidone iodine prior to surgery.
• Post-op antibiotics

q: Which of the following is the most important factor in the prevention of postoperative endophthalmitis?
o: One week antibiotics prior to surgery

Preoperative preparation with povidone iodine

• IOP & Retina examination
• Biometry for IOL power: SRK formula – A – 2.5L – 0.9k
• Femtosecond laser assisted cataract surgery: Most recent advancement
Medication history;
• Stop alpha blocker 3 days before surgery: As it can lead to Intra operative Iris syndrome/Floppy Iris syndrome
• Anaesthesia for PHACOEMULSIFICATION surgery: Mostly topical
• Risk of ENDOPHTHALMITIS: best prophylactic is 5% povidone iodine

q: How many weeks after cataract surgery are spectacles prescribed?

6 weeks
• Steroid eye drops are given after cataract surgery, in tapering doses over 4-6 weeks.
• Glasses are usually prescribed at the end of this period.

o: Prevention of formation of posterior synechiae

Ciliary muscle relaxation

• Atropine is the adjuvant drug that must be given in all cases of uveitis.

• Idiopathic: MC

q: A 25 year old male presents with central scotoma in the left eye. His right eye showed 6/6 vision. O/E, there is focal foveal detachment in the left eye. What should be the next step?

Inquire about use of steroids

q: A 2-week-old infant presents for evaluation due to a positive newborn screen for congenital hypothyroidism. The infant was born at term and has been feeding poorly. Physical examination reveals a lethargic infant with a large anterior fontanelle, hypotonia, and an umbilical hernia. Confirmatory laboratory tests show a markedly elevated serum TSH level and a decreased serum free T4 level. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this infant's hypothyroidism?
o: Inactivating mutation in the TSH receptor gene
e:
Most congenital hypothyroidism is due to thyroid dysgenesis (aplasia, hypoplasia or ectopic gland). High TSH with low T4 shows the problem is in the thyroid itself.
Key points
• Commonest cause worldwide of congenital hypothyroidism is thyroid dysgenesis; second is dyshormonogenesis.
• Features: lethargy, poor feeding, large fontanelle, umbilical hernia, prolonged jaundice, hoarse cry.
• Newborn screening: heel-prick TSH at 48-72 hours of age.
• Treat with oral levothyroxine as early as possible to protect brain development.

q: A 15-year-old adolescent presents with an anti-mongoloid slant, pulmonary stenosis, short stature, webbed neck, and undescended testis. What is the likely diagnosis?
e:
Short stature, webbed neck, pulmonary stenosis, undescended testis and an anti-mongoloid slant in a boy describe Noonan syndrome.
Key points
• Noonan syndrome has a normal karyotype (46 XY or XX) and is caused by RAS-MAPK gene mutations.
• Typical heart lesion is pulmonary stenosis; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy may also occur.
• Both sexes are affected; cryptorchidism is common, fertility in males may be reduced.
• Turner syndrome is 45 XO in girls with coarctation of aorta.
Noonan | Turner
Karyotype | Normal | 45 XO
Sex | Both | Female
