Gonads | Cryptorchidism | Streak ovary

q: Under the Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy, what is the recommended prophylactic dose and frequency of Iron and Folic Acid (IFA) supplementation for school-going children aged 5 to 9 years?
o: Daily 20 mg elemental iron + 100 mcg folic acid
Weekly 45 mg elemental iron + 400 mcg folic acid
Weekly 30 mg elemental on +250 mcg folic acid
e:
Under Anemia Mukt Bharat, school-age children (5-9 years) get weekly 45 mg elemental iron with 400 mcg folic acid (pink tablet).
Key points
• Anemia Mukt Bharat uses the 6x6x6 strategy: six age groups, six interventions, six institutional mechanisms.
• 6-59 months: biweekly IFA syrup, 20 mg iron plus 100 mcg folic acid.
• Adolescents and women also get weekly or daily IFA tablets as per age group.
• Other interventions: deworming, delayed cord clamping, fortified foods and testing with digital haemoglobinometers.
Age | Dose
6-59 mo | 20 mg Fe + 100 mcg FA, biweekly syrup
5-9 yr | 45 mg Fe + 400 mcg FA, weekly
10-19 yr | 60 mg Fe + 500 mcg FA, weekly

q:
A 20-month-old child diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) is receiving treatment in your clinic. Given below are five statements regarding the treatment. Pick out the incorrect statements.
1. Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be started from day 1 of admission.
2. The stabilization phase would ideally include the first seven days of treatment.
3. Vitamin A is given daily to overcome micronutrient deficiency.
4. F-75 feeds can be initiated in split portions.
5. Promote skin to skin contact with mother to avoid hypothermia.
e:
Statement 3 is wrong because vitamin A in SAM is given as a single age-appropriate dose, not daily. The other statements are correct.
Key points
• Antibiotics are given to all SAM children from day 1; amoxicillin if no complications, injectable if complicated.
• Stabilisation phase uses F-75 in small frequent feeds, 130 mL/kg/day, with 2-hourly feeding initially.
• Rehabilitation uses F-100 or RUTF with catch-up growth.
• Keep the child warm; skin to skin (kangaroo) contact prevents hypothermia.
• Give potassium and magnesium; avoid giving iron in the stabilisation phase.

q: A child is born with the following abnormality. What advice do you give to the mother, with regards to the next pregnancy?
o: 400 mcg of folic acid after confirmation of pregnancy
e:
The picture shows a neural tube defect (myelomeningocele). After one affected child, the next pregnancy needs high- dose 4000 mcg (4 mg) folic acid starting before conception.
Key points
• Neural tube closes by day 28 of gestation, often before the woman knows she is pregnant.
• General women planning pregnancy take 400 mcg folic acid daily, from 1 month before conception through 12 weeks.
• High dose (4 mg) is for previous NTD child, epilepsy on valproate or obesity.
• Serum alpha-fetoprotein and ultrasound are used for prenatal diagnosis of NTD.

q: The eldest child of a ragpicker from the urban slums of Bandra presents with severe lower limb pain. Examination reveals swelling of costochondral junctions. The X-ray image obtained is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
e:
Scurvy
Explanation
Severe limb pain with swollen costochondral junctions in an undernourished child with these knee X-ray changes is scurvy (vitamin C deficiency), due to subperiosteal bleeding.
Key points
Scurvy: bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhage, corkscrew hair, and painful pseudoparalysis. Painful limbs from subperiosteal bleeds; child lies in frog-leg position.
X-ray: ground-glass bone, pencil-thin cortex, white line of Frankel at metaphysis, Wimberger ring. Scorbutic rosary is angulated and painful; treat with vitamin C.
Scurvy | Rickets
Vitamin | C | D
Rosary | Sharp, painful | Round, painless
X-ray | White line | Cupping, fraying
Bleeding | Present | Absent

q: A 3-year-old boy presented to the clinic for a missed vaccination. His routine anthropometric measurements were noted. He was found to be 90 cms tall with a lower segment of 45 cm. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis in this child?
e:
Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia
Explanation
A 3-year-old with height 90 cm and lower segment 45 cm has an upper:lower segment ratio of 1.0, lower than the expected 1.3, so the trunk is short: spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia.
Key points
• Normal upper:lower segment ratio is 1.7 at birth, 1.3 at 3 years, and 1.0 after 7-10 years.
• Short-trunk dwarfism (SED) lowers the ratio; short-limb dwarfism (achondroplasia) raises it.
• Hypothyroidism and rickets keep the ratio raised (infantile proportions).
• Normal arm span equals height; in short trunk, arm span exceeds height.
US:LS | Type
Achondroplasia | High | Short limb
Hypothyroid | High | Short, stunted
SED | Low | Short trunk
Normal 3 yr | 1.3 | -

q: You notice a child pulling to the standing position and then shuffling around by holding onto furniture. At what age is this milestone typically attained?
e:
10 months
Explanation
Pulling up to stand and cruising around furniture is attained at about 10 months of age.
Key points
• Sits without support at 6 months; crawls at 8-9 months.
• Stands with support at 9 months; stands and cruises by 10 months.
• Walks alone at 12-13 months, climbs stairs holding at 15-18 months.
• Pincer grasp develops at 9-10 months.

q: A 2-year-old child is brought to the pediatric clinic. The mother reports that the child can run, walk up stairs two feet per step, stack 6 cubes, and combine 2 words into simple phrases (e.g., "want milk"). However, the child cannot jump off the ground with both feet or speak in 3-word sentences. What is the most appropriate assessment?
e:
Normal development for age
Explanation
Running, climbing stairs with two feet per step, stacking 6 cubes and two-word phrases are all expected at 2 years, so this is normal development.
Key points
• At 2 years: runs, kicks ball, builds a tower of 6 cubes, uses 2-word phrases.
• Jumping with both feet and 3-word sentences come at 3 years.
• Tower of 3 cubes is at 15 months; tower of 9 cubes at 3 years.
• Vocabulary at 2 years is about 50 words.

q: A 4-year-old child weighing 18 kg is admitted to the pediatric ward with mild acute gastroenteritis without signs of dehydration. Using the Holliday-Segar method, calculate the child's daily (24-hour) maintenance fluid requirement and the hourly fluid infusion rate.
e:
1400 mL/day; 58 mL/hr
Explanation
Holliday-Segar: first 10 kg = 1000 mL, next 8 kg x 50 = 400 mL, total 1400 mL/day, which is about 58 mL/hr.
Key points
• First 10 kg: 100 mL/kg/day.
• Next 10 kg: 50 mL/kg/day.
• Above 20 kg: 20 mL/kg/day.
• Hourly rate: 4 mL/kg/hr for first 10 kg, 2 mL/kg/hr next 10 kg, 1 mL/kg/hr after.

q: A toddler presented with progressive pallor and abdominal distention. On investigations, he had low hemoglobin. Which of the following red cell indices can be used to distinguish thalassemia from iron deficiency anemia?
o: Mean corpuscular volume/ Red blood cell count
e:
Mean corpuscular volume/ Red blood cell count
Explanation
The Mentzer index (MCV/RBC count) separates the two: below 13 favours thalassaemia, above 13 favours iron deficiency.
Key points
• Mentzer index: MCV divided by RBC count.
• In thalassaemia trait RBC count is high with low MCV; in iron deficiency RBC count is low.
• Confirm: HbA2 raised in beta thalassaemia trait; serum ferritin low in iron deficiency.
• Abdominal distension with pallor suggests hepatosplenomegaly in thalassaemia major.
Thalassaemia | Iron deficiency
Mentzer | Below 13 | Above 13
RBC count | Normal or high | Low
RDW | Normal | High
Ferritin | Normal | Low

q: The most common organism causing pneumonia in cystic fibrosis among the pediatric age group is _
e:
Staphylococcus aureus
Explanation
The commonest organism in cystic fibrosis pneumonia in children is Staphylococcus aureus; Pseudomonas takes over later with age.
Key points
• CF is autosomal recessive, caused by CFTR mutation (delta F508) on chromosome 7.
• Early childhood: Staph aureus and Haemophilus influenzae.
• Later childhood and adults: mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
• Burkholderia cepacia carries a bad prognosis; sweat chloride above 60 mEq/L diagnoses CF.

q: A first-time mother rushes to the OPD with her 4-day old infant and worriedly points to the rash that appears as shown below. You reassure her of its harmless, transient nature. On microscopic examination, these papular lesions on an erythematous base will reveal
e:
Eosinophils
Explanation
The picture shows erythema toxicum neonatorum, a harmless newborn rash whose lesions are packed with eosinophils on smear.
Key points
• Appears at 2-3 days of life, after 24 hours, and settles within a week.
• Papules and pustules on an erythematous base on trunk; spares palms and soles.
• It is the most common newborn rash and needs no treatment.
• Wright stain of pustule contents shows eosinophils.

q: A 6-day old infant is being examined. While checking the reflexes, a brisk reflex shown in the image is noted Which of the following conditions is a likely cause for this?
e:
Hypoglycemia
Explanation
The picture shows a brisk Moro reflex, which can be exaggerated in a jittery neonate with hypoglycaemia.
Key points
• Moro reflex: sudden head drop causes arm abduction and extension, then adduction.
• Present at birth, disappears by 3-6 months; persistence beyond this suggests brain damage.
• Asymmetric Moro suggests Erb's palsy or fractured clavicle.
• Moro is absent or weak in severe HIE and kernicterus.

q: A 2-day-old term neonate presents with severe cyanosis that does not improve despite 100% oxygen delivery On examination, S1 is single and loud, and no distinct murmur is heard. The electrocardiogram shows right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy. Chest X-ray shown below Which of the following is the immediate initial step in management?
e:
Intravenous Prostaglandin PGE_1 infusion
Explanation
Severe cyanosis not relieved by oxygen with an egg-on-side heart suggests transposition of the great arteries, and the first step is prostaglandin E1 infusion to keep the ductus open.
Key points
• TGA: aorta from right ventricle, pulmonary artery from left ventricle; cyanosis from day 1.
• Chest X-ray: egg on a string, narrow mediastinum, increased pulmonary vascularity.
• Balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind) is done next if mixing is poor.
• Definitive treatment: arterial switch operation in the first 2 weeks of life.
• Indomethacin closes the ductus; it is used in PDA of preterm babies.

q: A known case of substance abuse is brought to hospital with respiratory depression, bradycardia, hypothermia and pin point pupil. Emergency intravenous antidote was given to the patient. Which of the following drugs should be given for relapse prevention?
e:
• This is a case of Opioid poisoning.
• Antidote: I/V Naloxone
• Relapse prevention: Naltrexone
• Opioid withdrawal: Methadone
Explanation
Pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, bradycardia and hypothermia mean opioid poisoning. Naloxone is only the emergency antidote; naltrexone (long-acting oral opioid antagonist) is used for relapse prevention.
Key points
• Opioid toxicity triad: coma, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression.
• Naloxone: short-acting IV antidote, can precipitate withdrawal in dependent patients.
• Naltrexone: oral opioid antagonist for relapse prevention; also used in alcohol dependence.
• Methadone and buprenorphine are substitution (maintenance) therapy, not antidotes.
Naloxone | Naltrexone | Methadone
Action | Pure antagonist | Pure antagonist | Full agonist
Route | IV/IM | Oral | Oral
Use | Acute overdose | Relapse prevention | Maintenance, detox

q: A young man had a fight with his batchmates. The next day he started feeling that he is being followed by them and his brain is controlled by radio waves by his friends. He also complains of chest pain which he blames that his friends are sending some ultraviolet rays through mobile phones. The history is suggestive of;
e:
This is a case of SOMATIC PASSIVITY: Visceral hallucination – patient experiences certain somatic hallucinations which he believes are being imposed by some external agents.
Explanation
The patient feels that ultraviolet rays sent by others cause his chest pain, which is a bodily sensation imposed by an external agency. This is somatic passivity, a passivity phenomenon, and the radio-wave control of the brain fits the same pattern.
Key points
Passivity phenomena: patient feels body, thoughts, feelings or actions are controlled by outside force. Somatic passivity: bodily sensations are imposed by an external agent.
Passivity phenomena are first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia (Schneider).
Thought insertion: others put thoughts into the mind; here the complaint is a bodily sensation.
Somatic passivity | Thought insertion | Delusion of persecution
Feels imposed | Body sensation | Thoughts | Being harmed or followed
Example | Rays cause chest pain | Thoughts put in by others | Neighbours plan against me

q: A 50 year old man is brought to a psychiatrist with a 10 year history, that he suspects his neighbours and he feels that whenever he passes by they sneeze and plan against him behind his back. He feels that his wife has been replaced by a double and calls police for help. Sometimes he uses multiple metaphors and new terms which no one has heard before. He is quite well-groomed, alert, occasionally consumes alcohol. What is the likely diagnosis?
e:
• Delusion of persecution + Neologism + Capgrass syndrome + Preserved personality = Paranoid Schizophrenia
• Diagnostic criteria:
• ≥ 2 symptoms ≥ 1 month (ICD-11)
• ≥ 2 symptoms ≥ 6 months (DSM-5)
Explanation
Persecutory delusion, neologisms, Capgras delusion and preserved personality and grooming for 10 years point to paranoid schizophrenia. Hebephrenic type has disorganised behaviour and early onset; paranoid personality has no psychotic delusions.
Key points
• Paranoid schizophrenia: delusions and hallucinations with relatively preserved personality and cognition.
• Capgras: belief that a close person has been replaced by a double.
• Neologism: patient makes up new words; a formal thought disorder.
• Diagnosis: symptoms for at least 1 month (ICD); DSM-5 needs total illness of 6 months.
Paranoid | Hebephrenic
Onset | Late (25-35 y) | Early (15-25 y)
Main feature | Delusions, hallucinations | Disorganised, silly behaviour
Prognosis | Better | Worse

q: A 58 year old man is brought by his wife. He thinks that he has committed sins throughout his life. He is very much depressed and has considered committing suicide but has not taken any such steps. He is also taking sessions with a spiritual guru. He does not get convinced when his wife tells him that he has led a pious life. What is the better modality of treatment?
o: Guidance and recounselling with spiritual guru with antidepressant
e:
This is a case of psychotic depression.
Explanation
Fixed delusion of guilt and sin that does not change with reassurance, plus depression and suicidal thoughts, is psychotic depression. It needs an antipsychotic with an antidepressant (or ECT); antidepressant alone or counselling is not enough.
Key points
• Psychotic depression: major depression with mood-congruent delusions such as guilt, sin, nihilism.
• Treatment: antidepressant plus antipsychotic; ECT is very effective.
• ECT is preferred when suicide risk is high.
• Delusion of guilt and Cotard (nihilistic) delusion occur in severe depression.

q: A 40 year old female, nondiabetic, non-hypertensive patient has some extra beats in pulse. Doctor informed that it is benign and no intervention is required. But she is worried that it is a serious cardiac disorder and is still going for repeated investigations and consulting many doctors. This is a case of;
e:
She is persistently worried about a serious illness despite doctor's reassurance and normal findings, and keeps doctor- shopping. This is hypochondriasis (illness anxiety disorder). Factitious illness involves deliberately faking symptoms.
Key points
• Hypochondriasis: fear of having a serious disease based on misinterpreting normal body sensations.
• Reassurance does not help; repeated investigations and doctor shopping are common.
• Somatic symptom disorder: distressing physical symptoms, with excessive thoughts and behaviour.
• Factitious disorder: symptoms intentionally produced for the sick role; no external gain.
Hypochondriasis | Factitious | Malingering
Symptoms | Not produced, feared | Produced consciously | Produced consciously
Motive | Anxiety | Sick role | External gain

q: A radiographer stands 1 metre from an X-ray source during a portable chest radiograph in the ICU. To reduce his radiation exposure, he steps back so that he is 3 metres from the source. By what factor is the intensity of radiation reaching him reduced?
e:
• Inverse square law: intensity of radiation is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source (I ∝ 1/d²).
• Tripling the distance (1 m → 3 m) reduces intensity by 3² = 9 times; doubling the distance reduces it 4 times.
• Distance is the simplest and most effective protection measure, along with time and shielding (ALARA principle).
• Lead aprons (0.25–0.5 mm lead equivalent) and thyroid shields protect staff working near the source.
• ICRP dose limits: 20 mSv/year for radiation workers (averaged over 5 years); 1 mSv/year for the public.

q: A male newborn has a palpable bladder and a poor, dribbling urinary stream. Antenatal ultrasound had shown bilateral hydronephrosis, a thick-walled distended bladder with a dilated posterior urethra and oligohydramnios. Which is the investigation of choice to evaluate this condition?

q: A 45-year-old man with blunt chest trauma is breathless. His erect chest X-ray shows a hyperlucent left hemithorax with absent lung markings laterally, a visible collapsed lung edge, and a horizontal air-fluid level at the base. What is the most likely diagnosis?

- Left side commoner after blunt trauma – but no lung edge.

q: A 2-year-old boy from a low-income family is brought with delayed walking and bowing of both legs. Examination shows widened wrists and a row of beads along the costochondral junctions. X-ray of the wrist shows cupping and fraying of the distal radial metaphysis. Which set of laboratory findings is most likely?
o: Low calcium, high phosphate, low ALP
Low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high ALP
High calcium, low phosphate, normal ALP
Normal calcium, normal phosphate, normal ALP
e:
Low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high ALP
• Delayed walking, bow legs, widened wrists, rachitic rosary + metaphyseal cupping/fraying = nutritional rickets
• Labs: calcium low/normal, phosphate low, ALP raised (earliest and best screening marker), PTH raised, Vit D low.
• X-ray: cupping, fraying, splaying of metaphysis, widened growth plate;
• Earliest sign = loss of the zone of provisional calcification.
• Rickety rosary is rounded and painless (scorbutic rosary is sharp and tender).
Differentiating each option
A. Low calcium, high phosphate, low ALP
- Low Ca + high PO4+Normal ALP = hypoparathyroidism
- Low Ca + high PO4+High ALP= renal osteodystrophy.
- Low ALP with rickets-like bones = hypophosphatasia
B. Low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high ALP
- Classic pattern of vitamin D-deficiency rickets with secondary hyperparathyroidism.
- Same pattern with normal PTH & normal vitamin D → X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets.
C. High calcium, low phosphate, normal ALP
- High Ca + low PO4 = primary hyperparathyroidism
D. Normal calcium, normal phosphate, normal ALP
- All-normal labs: physiological bowing (normal till ~2 yr), Blount disease, osteoporosis.
- X-ray would not show cupping/fraying or widened physis.

q: A 23-year-old RTA patient with a closed fracture of the femoral shaft, managed on traction, becomes restless and confused 48 hours after the injury. He is breathless with SpO 2 of 86% on room air, and a petechial rash appears over his upper chest, axillae and conjunctivae. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e:
Fat embolism syndrome
• Long-bone (femur) or pelvic fracture + onset 24–72 h + hypoxaemia + confusion + petechiae = fat embolism syndrome
• Gurd major criteria: respiratory insufficiency, cerebral signs, petechial rash
Minor: tachycardia, fever, retinal emboli, jaundice, renal signs, fall in Hb/platelets, raised ESR.
• The petechial rash is the most specific sign.
• Investigations: fat globules in urine/sputum, thrombocytopenia,
• “snowstorm” chest X-ray
• “starfield” pattern on DW MRI of Brain .

q: A 6-year-old boy falls on his outstretched hand from a swing. His elbow is swollen with a S shaped deformity`, the three-point bony relationship is maintained, and the radial pulse is feeble. He cannot flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb. What is the most likely injury?

Extension-type supracondylar fracture of the humerus

• Child + FOOSH + swollen elbow with S-shaped deformity + three-point bony relationship maintained = supracondylar fracture of humerus (commonest elbow fracture in children, peak 5 –7 yr).
• Extension type ≈ 95% (distal fragment displaced posteriorly);
• Nerve injury: AIN commonest overall (cannot flex thumb IP / make the “OK” sign).
• Feeble pulse = brachial artery compromise
• Complications: Volkmann ischaemic contracture
• cubitus varus / gunstock deformity
• myositis ossificans.
Differentiating each option
A. Posterior dislocation of the elbow
- Three-point relationship LOST
- Terrible triad of Elbow -DRC Dislocated Elbow
Radial head fracture
Coronoid process fracture
B. Fracture of the lateral condyle of the humerus
- 2nd commonest paediatric elbow fracture;
- three-point relationship disturbed.
- Non-union
- cubitus valgus → tardy ulnar nerve palsy;
C. Pulled elbow (radial head subluxation)
- Age 1–4 yr, sudden pull on the hand; no swelling or deformity; arm held pronated.
- X-ray normal;
- reduce by immediate supination + flexion
D. Extension-type supracondylar fracture of the humerus
- S-shaped deformity + intact three-point relationship + vascular and AIN signs =
extension-type supracondylar fracture.

q: A 25-year-old wrestler presents after a fall with his arm held slightly abducted and externally rotated. The shoulder looks flattened off and he has lost sensation over the lower lateral aspect of the deltoid. Which nerve is injured?
e:
Axillary nerve
• Arm abducted + externally rotated with a flattening of shoulder (loss of deltoid contour, prominent acromion) = anterior shoulder dislocation (MC type,subcoracoid commonest).
• Nerve injured = axillary nerve → numbness over the regimental badge area, deltoid weakness.
• Clinical tests: Hamilton ruler test, Dugas test, Bryant sign (lowered axillary fold), Callaway test.
• Lesions causing recurrence: Bankart (anteroinferior labrum – “essential lesion”) and Hill–Sachs (posterolateral humeral head defect)
• Reduction: Kocher (traction → external rotation → adduction → internal rotation)
• Posterior dislocation follows epileptic fits/electric shock: arm adducted + internally rotated, “electric-bulb” sign.
Differentiating each option
A. Musculocutaneous nerve
- C5–C7; weak elbow flexion & supination, lost biceps jerk.
- Sensory loss over lateral forearm, not the deltoid – rarely injured in dislocation.
B. Radial nerve
- Wrist drop + finger drop,
- numb first dorsal web space.
- Seen with shaft of humerus fracture
- Crutch / Saturday-night palsy.
C. Axillary nerve
- Anterior dislocation stretches the nerve around the surgical neck → regimental badge anaesthesia.
D. Long thoracic nerve
- Supplies serratus anterior → winging of scapula (push against wall).
- Pure motor – no sensory loss;
- injured in axillary surgery during radical mastectomy / heavy backpack.

q: A 32-year-old man falls on his outstretched hand. His wrist is swollen with a prominent ulnar head. X-ray shows a displaced fracture at the junction of the middle and distal thirds of the radius with dislocation of the distal radio-ulnar joint. What is this injury called?
e:
Galeazzi fracture-dislocation
• Fracture at the junction of middle and distal thirds of radius + DRUJ dislocation = Galeazzi fracture-dislocation (“reverse Monteggia”).
• “Fracture of necessity” → ORIF with plating
Differentiating each option
A. Monteggia fracture-dislocation
- Fracture proximal third of ULNA + radial head dislocation.
- Bado type I (anterior) commonest; PIN palsy
B. Galeazzi fracture-dislocation
- Distal-third radius fracture + DRUJ disruption
C. Essex-Lopresti injury
- Comminuted radial head fracture + interosseous membrane tear + DRUJ injury.
- Proximal migration of radius – never excise radial head alone.
D. Barton fracture
- Intra-articular fracture of distal radius (dorsal or volar) with carpal subluxation.
- Colles – dorsal tilt, dinner-fork;
- Smith – volar, garden-spade.

q:
A 68-year-old woman presents with sudden back pain after lifting a bucket of water. X-ray shows a wedge compression fracture of L1.
DEXA scan shows a T-score of −2.8 at the lumbar spine.
Serum calcium, phosphate and ALP are normal. How is her condition classified?
e:
Severe osteoporosis
• WHO DEXA criteria (T-score):
• ≥ −1.0 normal;
• −1.0 to −2.5 osteopenia;
• ≤ −2.5 osteoporosis;
• ≤ −2.5 plus a fragility fracture = severe (established) osteoporosis.
• Use Z-score (age-matched) for premenopausal women, men <50 and children.
• DEXA of hip and lumbar spine = gold standard;
• Labs are normal in primary osteoporosis
• Fragility fractures: vertebral (commonest), hip, distal radius (Colles).
• Treatment: calcium + vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, fall prevention; bisphosphonates first line (alendronate, zoledronic acid); Bisphosphonate risks: osteonecrosis of jaw, atypical femoral fracture.
Differentiating each option
A. Normal bone density
- T-score ≥ −1.0.
B. Osteopenia
- T-score between −1.0 and −2.5.
C. Osteoporosis
- T-score ≤ −2.5 without a fragility fracture.
D. Severe (established) osteoporosis
- T-score ≤ −2.5 + fragility fracture (vertebra).

q: A 28-year-old man is admitted after a severe road traffic accident with a devastating traumatic brain injury. Despite maximal neurocritical care, brain death is formally declared according to the required criteria. His family consents to organ donation, and he is transferred to the operating room for multiorgan procurement for transplantation. What is the appropriate ASA Physical Status classification for this patient?
e:
ASA VI
Declared brain death + organ removal for donor purposes = ASA VI.
Miller ’s ASA-PS classification specifically defines ASA VI as a declared brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donor purposes.
Golden Points
ASA 1 → Healthy
ASA 2 → Mild systemic disease
ASA 3 → Severe systemic disease
ASA 4 → Severe disease + constant threat to life ASA
5 → Moribund; will not survive without surgery ASA
6 → Brain-dead organ donor
“E” → Emergency surgery

q: A 56-year-old man is scheduled for elective surgery under general anaesthesia. During the pre-anaesthesia machine check, the anaesthesiologist decides to attach a backup E-cylinder to the anaesthesia workstation. The hanger yoke accepts a cylinder with a Pin Index Safety System (PISS) configuration of 2 and 5. Which of the following is the correct shoulder and body colour of this cylinder according to the traditional Indian medical-gas cylinder colour coding?
e:
White shoulder with black body
Pin index 2,5 → Oxygen cylinder.
The Pin Index Safety System prevents accidental interchange of medical gas cylinders by providing a gas-specific pin arrangement at the hanger yoke.
Oxygen → White shoulder + Black body.
Golden Points
Air
O2 → PISS 2,5 → White shoulder + Black body
N2O → PISS 3,5 → Blue shoulder + Blue body
CO2 → PISS 1,6 → Grey shoulder + Grey body
PISS = Cylinder safety system
DISS = Pipeline/hose connection safety system

q: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a high-speed road traffic accident. He has signs of intra-abdominal hemorrhage and requires an emergency exploratory laparotomy. Because of worsening consciousness and inadequate ventilation, general anesthesia is induced and tracheal intubation is attempted. Despite optimized laryngoscopy and alternative intubation attempts, tracheal intubation fails. Two- person face-mask ventilation is inadequate, and placement of a supraglottic airway device also fails to provide effective ventilation. The patient's SpO 2 is rapidly falling despite administration of 100% oxygen. The patient is now in a cannot-intubate, cannot-oxygenate/ventilate airway emergency. What is the most appropriate immediate airway intervention?
e:
Cricothyrotomy
• This is a CICO/CICV emergency: intubation has failed and adequate oxygenation cannot be achieved by either face mask or supraglottic airway.
• Miller describes the difficult-airway emergency pathway as proceeding to an emergency invasive airway when nonsurgical airway techniques fail to achieve adequate oxygenation. Cricothyrotomy is specifically included as an emergency invasive technique after rescue maneuvers have failed or are not feasible.
Golden Points
• Cannot intubate + cannot oxygenate → Emergency invasive airway
• Cricothyrotomy → preferred in dire, time-critical emergency because it is rapid
• Tracheostomy → generally slower; better for non-time-critical situations

q: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed road traffic accident. He is pale, restless, and diaphoretic, with cold extremities and delayed capillary refill. His vital signs are: Heart rate: 136/min, Blood pressure: 76/42 mmHg, Respiratory rate: 30/min, SpO 2: 95% with supplemental oxygen Abdominal examination reveals marked distension, guarding, and diffuse tenderness. FAST examination shows free intraperitoneal fluid in the hepatorenal and splenorenal recesses. Blood-product resuscitation is initiated, but the patient remains markedly hypotensive. The surgical team decides to proceed immediately with an emergency exploratory laparotomy for suspected ongoing intra-abdominal hemorrhage. Rapid-sequence induction of general anaesthesia is planned. Which of the following is the most appropriate anaesthetic induction agent in this patient?
e:
Ketamine
This patient has major blood loss with severe hypotension and compensatory tachycardia. Miller states that ketamine is frequently used for induction in hypotensive trauma patients because its centrally mediated sympathetic stimulation and catecholamine release tend to support cardiovascular function.
Golden Points
• Ketamine → NMDA receptor Antagonist, produces dissociative anaesthesia.
• Etomidate → Cardiovascular stability, causes adrenal suppression.
• Thiopentone → contraindicated in acute intermittent porphyria because barbiturates induce hepatic enzymes and can precipitate an attack.

q: A 55-year-old man undergoes elective abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia. Pancuronium is administered intraoperatively to provide skeletal muscle relaxation. At the end of surgery, neuromuscular monitoring demonstrates residual blockade. The anaesthesiologist administers an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor to reverse the neuromuscular block. Soon afterward, the patient develops marked bradycardia, pupillary constriction, excessive salivation, diarrhea, and urinary incontinence. Which of the following drugs can be used to decrease the effects caused by anti acetylcholinesterase?
e:
Glycopyrrolate
The acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used here is neostigmine. By inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, neostigmine increases acetylcholine not only at nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction, but also at muscarinic receptors, producing unwanted parasympathetic effects.
Glycopyrrolate: It is an antimuscarinic drug commonly paired with
neostigmine to counteract bradycardia and other muscarinic effects.
Golden Points
• Neostigmine → acetylcholinesterase inhibitor → ↑ acetylcholine
• Neostigmine reverses nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade
• Muscarinic effects → bradycardia + salivation + bronchial secretions + GI/urinary activity
• Neostigmine + Glycopyrrolate → classic reversal combination
• Sugammadex → reverses rocuronium/vecuronium; not clinically useful for pancuronium reversal
• Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) → 20% Intralipid / lipid emulsion therapy.

q: A 32-year-old man has well-demarcated erythematous plaques with thick silvery-white scales over both elbows, knees and the scalp. Gentle scraping of a plaque produces pinpoint bleeding spots. New lesions have appeared along a recent scratch mark. What is the pinpoint bleeding sign called?
e:
Auspitz sign
• Clinical picture of erythematous plaques with thick silvery-white scales over both elbows, knees and the scalp point towards chronic plaque psoriasis
• Auspitz sign: pinpoint bleeding on removing scales - due to dilated tortuous capillaries in elongated dermal papillae with suprapapillary thinning.
• Lesions along trauma = Koebner (isomorphic) phenomenon;
• Grattage test: candle-grease scaling on scraping.
• HPE: Munro microabscesses, parakeratosis, regular acanthosis;
• nails show pitting, oil-drop sign, onycholysis.
Differentiating each option
A. Koebner phenomenon
- New lesions at sites of trauma (isomorphic response) – present in psoriasis too, but it is not the bleeding sign.
- Also seen in lichen planus, vitiligo, warts.
B. Auspitz sign
- Pinpoint bleeding on removing scales = Auspitz sign of psoriasis.
- Grattage sequence: candle-grease sign -> Burkley membrane -> Auspitz sign.
C. Nikolsky sign
- Epidermis shears off with lateral pressure – pemphigus, TEN, SSSS.
- Psoriasis is Nikolsky negative – epidermis is not fragile.
D. Darier sign
- Itching,Erythema and Edema seen in – urticaria pigmentosa (mastocytosis).

q: A 40-year-old woman has intensely itchy, flat-topped, shiny, violaceous polygonal papules over the flexor aspect of both wrists. On close examination the papules show fine white lacy lines on their surface, and similar white reticulate lesions are present on the buccal mucosa. What are these white lines called?
e:
Wickham striae
• Lichen planus - 6 Ps: Planar, Purple, Polygonal, Pruritic, Papules and Plaques; flexor wrists, shins.
• Wickham striae: white lacy lines due to focal hypergranulosis.
• HPE: saw-tooth rete ridges, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate, Civatte (colloid) bodies, hypergranulosis.
• Associated with hepatitis C;
• nails show pterygium;
• oral lichen planus has malignant potential.
Differentiating each option
A. Wickham striae
- Fine white lacy lines over LP papules and buccal mucosa = Wickham striae (focal hypergranulosis).
B. Beau lines
- Transverse nail grooves after severe illness / chemotherapy (temporary arrest of nail growth).
- Affect the nails, not skin papules or mucosa.
C. Pastia lines
- Linear petechiae in skin folds in scarlet fever.
- Accompanied by sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor.
D. Muehrcke lines
- Paired white transverse nail bands – hypoalbuminaemia (nephrotic syndrome).

q: A 50-year-old woman presents with painful oral erosions for 2 months followed by flaccid blisters on the trunk that rupture easily, leaving raw areas. Gentle pressure on normal-looking skin next to a blister makes the epidermis slide off. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin would show which pattern?
o: Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone
Granular IgA in the dermal papillae
Intercellular IgG in a "fishnet" pattern within the epidermis
Linear IgA along the basement membrane
e:
Intercellular IgG in a "fishnet" pattern within the epidermis
• Pemphigus vulgaris: oral lesions first, blisters,bullae,skin erosions,
• Nikolsky sign positive, bulla-spread (Asboe-Hansen) sign.
• Autoantibodies (IgG) against desmoglein 3
• intraepidermal, suprabasal blister with acantholysis ("row of tombstones").
• Tzanck smear: acantholytic cells;
• DIF: intercellular IgG / C3 "fishnet" (chicken-wire) pattern.
• Treatment: systemic corticosteroids + rituximab
Differentiating each option
A. Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone
- Bullous pemphigoid – tense subepidermal bullae in the elderly, Nikolsky negative.
- Blister is subepidermal;
- oral lesions uncommon.
B. Granular IgA in the dermal papillae
- Dermatitis herpetiformis – grouped itchy vesicles on extensors; celiac disease.
- Intensely itchy; blisters
- no oral erosions.
C. Intercellular IgG in a "fishnet" pattern within the epidermis
- Anti-desmoglein IgG between keratinocytes = pemphigus vulgaris.
- oral lesions first + flaccid bullae + Nikolsky positive.
D. Linear IgA along the basement membrane
- Linear IgA bullous dermatosis – 'string of pearls' blisters;
- Seen in children (chronic bullous disease of childhood)

q: A 22-year-old athlete notices multiple scaly hypopigmented macules over the upper chest and back that become more obvious after sun exposure. KOH mount of the scales shows short hyphae and round yeast cells. What is the causative organism?
e:
Malassezia furfur
• Pityriasis (tinea) versicolor: caused by Malassezia spp. - a lipophilic yeast;
• Hypo- or hyperpigmented, finely scaly macules on the upper trunk; scales become visible on scratching .
• KOH: "spaghetti and meatballs" ;
• Wood lamp: yellow-orange fluorescence.
• Hypopigmentation due to azelaic acid (inhibits tyrosinase);
• treatment: topical ketoconazole / selenium sulphide,
Differentiating each option
A. Trichophyton rubrum
- Commonest dermatophyte – tinea corporis / cruris, onychomycosis; annular plaques;
- KOH: septate hyphae.
B. Malassezia furfur
- KOH 'spaghetti and meatballs' + scaly hypopigmented macules = pityriasis versicolor.
- Wood lamp: yellow-orange fluorescence.
C. Candida albicans
- Intertrigo with satellite pustules, oral thrush;
- KOH: budding yeast + pseudohyphae.
- Prefers moist flexures
D. Microsporum canis
- Zoophilic (cats / dogs) – tinea capitis / corporis in children;
- Wood lamp green fluorescence of infected hairs.

q: A 28-year-old man takes co-trimoxazole for a urinary infection. Within a few hours he develops a single, well-defined, round, dusky violaceous plaque with a central blister on the glans penis. He recalls an identical lesion at exactly the same site after taking the same drug a year ago, which healed with dark pigmentation. What is the diagnosis?
e:
Fixed drug eruption
• Fixed drug eruption: recurs at the same site every time the drug is taken;
• Heals with residual post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation;
• common sites: genitalia (glans), lips, hands.
• Common drugs: sulphonamides (co-trimoxazole), NSAIDs, tetracyclines, phenytoin, barbiturates.
• Diagnosis by history / oral provocation test;
• treatment: stop the drug, topical steroids.
• Herpes gives grouped painful vesicles (Tzanck: multinucleated giant cells).
Differentiating each option
A. Fixed drug eruption
- Recurrence at the same site with the same drug + residual pigmentation = FDE.
- Commonest sites: genitalia, lips;
- biopsy shows pigment incontinence.
B. Erythema multiforme
- Multiple symmetrical target lesions on acral sites; usually HSV-triggered; not fixed to one site.
- Lesions are multiple and symmetrical, not solitary.
C. Herpes genitalis
- Recurrent Genital Grouped painful vesicles / erosions;
- Tzanck: multinucleated giant cells.
D. Stevens-Johnson syndrome
- Mucocutaneous lesions < 10%
- onset 1-3 weeks after the drug.
- does not recur at one fixed site.
